The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) moved that the House go into committee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, That it is expedient to make provision for a subsidy, not exceeding $133,333.33 a year, for a steamship service between Canada and France.
Motion agreed to.

House again in committee on the resolution :
That it is expedient, in connection with the Bill now before this House, respecting the construction of a national transcontinental railway, to ratify the agreement set forth in the schedule to the said Bill, entered into on the 28th of July, 1903, between the government and certain persons on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, a company to be incorporated by parliament at the present session thereof, and to authorize the government to do whatever is necessary to give full effect to the said Bill and' agreement.-The Prime Minister.

I think that the best way to get through the subject-matter of this resolution would be to read over the agreement and take it clause by clause. This would concentrate criticism or inquiry, and would facilitate the work of the committee. I think this would be the most expeditious way.

I would suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that we should' take this stage and have the discussion upon the second reading and on the committee stage of the Bill. If agreeable to my hon. friend, we will take this motion simply formally to-day, report the resolution and set down the Bill for discussion to-morrow, say, and have the discussion in Committee of the Whole on the Bill.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Personally, I have no great objection to that course. But I do not know how far my colleagues on this side of the House are prepared for it. My right hon. friend announced that the business of today would be taking up in examining this agreement, and we have prepared in consequence. If we are going to take up other business, what is it to be ? Perhaps, having prepared in accordance with the Prime Minister's announcement, we may not be ready for the course which he would now propose.
If my hon. friend is prepared to go on with this, we will go on with it.
Very well.
I think I can meet the suggestion of my hon. friend. Let the resolution be put; then move the second reading of the Bill, and have the discussion upon It.
There will be no limit in that case, I suppose, to the latitude granted to members of the committee to discuss the Bill generally, not only specially the clauses of the Bill ?

The whole thing would come up.
The MINISTER OP FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding,!. In committee.

Resolution reported ; read the first and second times ; agreed to, and referred to the Committee of the Whole on Bill 235.
The PRIME MINISTER moved the second reading of Bill (No. 235) to provide for the construction of a national transcontinental railway.
Motion agreed to ; and Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2,
The said agreement bearing date the 29th day of July, 1903, a copy of which forms the schedule to this Act, is hereby ratified and confirmed, and declared to be legally binding upon His Majesty and the said Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and His Majesty and the said Company are hereby authorized and empowered to do whatever is necessary in order to give full effect to the said agreement.

Upon this clause I think it would be advantageous for the committee to get some information of a precise nature as to where the line is going to pass. Of course, after the very lengthy discussion that has taken place in regard to the Bill itself and the agreement as a whole, there are certain facts which cannot now be controverted. The line has not been explored, the line has not been localized, it has not been possible to do that, I suppose. It is utterly impossible for us who are called upon to vote upon this important agreement, to say within a certain number of miles where that line is going to pass. We must take the conditions as they are. But what seems to me very important is that, before passing upon this agreement, we should know at any rate within 100 miles, where the line is going to pass. Take the western section coming eastward from the Rocky mountains to Winnipeg. There are two lines there already, one built and the other partially built. Now the object of this portion of the line-and I w-ill confine my remarks for the purpose of order and simplicity to that part only at present-is both to open up the fertile part of the North-west, and, without in any way injuring the existing or projected lines, to invade, if I may use that expression, the most fertile and available part of the wheat producing belt in the North-west. Our interest in- that part of the line consists in the guarantee ; the whole guarantee upon the line from Winnipeg to the Rocky mountains amounts to a very considerable sum, and it seems to me of the utmost importance that we should know -about where that portion of the line is going to pass, under what latitude, how that projected line in which we are so vitally interested financially and otherwise, is going to be situated in reference to the other lines that I have mentioned. We should be able to judge of the position of that line in order to appreciate its usefulness in that part of the country, and in order to do that, when we approach the consideration of the east-

era section, winch the government intends to build, we should be able to compare the situation of the line built by the Grand Trunk Pacific with the line built by the government, and so to form a clear judgment of the advantage of the whole line as a transcontinental route, as a great freight route from west to east. We will then be better able, later on, to consider this whole measure and to appreciate its value in the east as a colonization line. But just at present it seems to me that it is due to the committee that the government should be able, proceeding from west to east, from the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains to Winnipeg, to tell us about where the line is going to be situated. Some doubt has been expressed as to whether it is possible for that line to pass north of the Canadian Northern. I have heard the opinion expressed that it was intended that the line should pass between the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway west of Winnipeg. I think it is due to the committee that the government should tell us approximately at least-It is very unfortunate that the line has not been localized, and we are not in a position to say precisely where it is going to pass-I think we should know approximately at least how it is going to lie in that great western region, and that we should have information upon that point before we take up the important question of the locality of the line north of Lake Superior, its situation in the province of Ontario and its situation in the province of Quebec. I think we should get information just now upon that point.

I cannot but believe that my hon. friend, on reflection, will be forced to admit that the request which he now makes is one which cannot be granted under any circumstances whatever. The Act of incorporation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has been settled by parliament, and the line has been located by Act of parliament as nearly as it is possible to do so before the actual location has been fixed on the ground. Every day we grant charters to companies for building railways, and the only thing that parliament can do under such circumstances is simply to fix certain points between where there should be communication. But it goes without saying, and everybody knows, that between those points the actual surveys may change, and vary what has been at first blush considered to be the probable route. Conditions may be found on the ground which may force the company to deviate from the course at first intended, and may force it to take another one. In the present case I would call the attention of the committee to the precedent of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When the contract was made with the Canadian Pacigo through Canada to the Pacific ocean, there was not even any point mentioned on the Pacific ocean which was to be the terminus. The terminus might have been at Port Moody, as it was contemplated at one time, it might have been at Burrard, as it was afterwards determined, it might have been at Bute Inlet, it might have been at Port Simpson, or any other place. In this contract we have, as approximately as we could, located the very point which must fie the terminus. We have also located, as far as that section is concerned, the line the railway must take in saying that it must proceed westward from Winnipeg to Port Simpson, and to touch at certain points on the way, amongst others at Edmonton, then to go as directly as possible to Port Simpson. But it is impossible to say of that whole length that the line must go here or there. My hon. friend says that he has heard rumours to the effect that the line was to pass between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern. I must say that I have been surprised at the credulity which our hon. friends opposite have attached to rumours. This is not the only rumour which my hon. friend hears, there are a good many others, and there is no more foundation in the one than in the other.	.
There is no more foundation for the statement that it is the intention of the government to locate the line between the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the line of the Canadian Northern Railway than there is to say that it is their intention that the line shall pass north of the Canadian Northern Railway. For my part I should imagine, looking at the information I have at present on the subject, that it might be more convenient that this line should go north and thus extend as far as possible the area of cultivable lands ; because we know there is ample room for settlement in that northern country, and therefore room for more railway accommodation. But at this present juncture it would not be possible for the government to decide. And I say positively that the government has not come, and cannot come to any conclusion on that subject until we have completed the surveys which must be a preliminary condition to the construction of this road. The first thing which the government must do, and the first thing which the Grand Trunk Railway must do, is to have actual professional surveys made in order to ascertain the best location for the line. I understand that there are engineers who make a specialty of locating lines of railway, men who understand the topography of a given country, and wlio are able to find in that country the best topographical route for the location of a railway. That is a professional acquirement and this professional skill has to be exercised, the surveys have to take place, before it will be possible to say exactly
I would refic Railway syndicate, the only direction which was given them was that they should * where the line will be located.

mind the House of the condition which was enjoined upon this company when it was granted a charter, a condition by which the government will have to abide, and which cannot be discarded. A stipulation was made by this House when the charter was granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway that wherever it locates its line, whether on the south or on the north of the existing railways, it must place it, except at terminal points, at a distance of at least thirty miles from any existing railways or from any railways that have been located. Beyond this I do not think it is possible to give any further information to the House.

What the right hon. Premier has said only goes to confirm what has been stated more than once during this discussion, that we really have no information and that the mountains of information that my right hon. friend boasted he could place at tlie disposal of this House amount to nothing whatever. I venture to say this, that although I am not as conversant with the situation in the west as with that in the east, if my right hon. friend thinks we are going to pass over the eastern section of the line in the province of Ontario and in the province of Quebec without having more precise information than that, he will find that his lack of information will militate against expeditiousness in the discussion of this measure. Now what does my right hon. friend say ? His argument, as I understand it, was this :	A private Bill has
been passed authorizing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to construct a line between a certain point and another point; that Bill has been debated in the House and it is not our business to go any further into the question of the location of the line, although this is the first opportunity we, as representatives of the people, have had of asking where the line is going to pass. We are now considering a grant to a great transcontinental road, and our position is quite different from the position which we occupied when this company applied to us for incorporation, and for power to construct this railway. The position is entirely altered, and it becomes our duty now, when we are voting money to a line which purports to be the best possible transcontinental line, to find out where that line is going to pass, so that the argument of my right hon. friend does not seem to apply at all. My right hon. friend says that a similar lack of information existed at the time the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed. The circumstances then were entirely different. We were then building the first line into an unknown country, and at that time, speaking generally, one might say it mattered very little where the line was going to pass so long as it crossed the prairies and connected British Columbia with the rest of the Dominion. Now we have two lines in existence, and the question is:	Where are we going to locate the

third ? I do not see what ground our right hon. friend has for saying that we are very credulous when we accept the statement that has been made that this line would pass between the two present existing lines, the Canadian Northern Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. A glance at a map is sufficient to show that it is very difficult for this line to pass anywhere else. I believe myself, with the limited knowledge I have at my disposal, with the mole hills of information I can command at the present moment, that the proper location for this line would be for it to pass north of the Canadian Northern Railway in order that there should not be too many lines in that district. Is my right hon. friend able to say whether it passes between the two lines or north of the Canadian Northern Railway ? The promoters of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway represented to the Railway Committee, if I remember rightly, that the preliminary surveys of that portion had been made ; we know that last summer the officers of the company were engaged in work in that region. Surely under these circumstances the government should be able to tell us approximately where the line is going to pass. The Canadian Northern Railway is, I believe, intended to go from Winnipeg to Grandview ; and from Grandview to Saskatoon, and thence to Edmonton. The Canadian Pacific Railway starting from Brandon passes through Regina, Medicine Hat and Macleod. There is a vast region lying between these two lines, and I ask if it is intended that this line should pass through that region. Or is it intended that the road should pass directly north in the Saskatchewan district. Surely we are entitled to know that. Is this line going to pass through Dunvegan V These are pertinent questions, and my hon. friends from the west who are more familiar with the country may not require more precise information, but it seems to me that when an hon. member rises in this committee on an important measure of this kind, and seeks to ascertain within three or four hundred miles where a line, greatly aided by the government, is going to pass, a line Intended both to colonize this large district and to serve as a quick transportation route and he is told by the government that they are not able to say within 300 or 400 or 500 miles where that line is going to pass, that the question even seems irrelevant, and that it is after this committee has voted very substantial aid to that part of the transcontinental road, long after all the experts and officials have passed over the ground and determined where the line is going to be located that this information is to be given us-I say, without exaggeration, that it seems to me to be absolutely making fun of the committee. I admit that as things are now it is no use crying over spilt milk ; or going over the ground that has already been traversed time and again. We are

treating with a company whose line is not precisely located, but it seems to me that my right hon. friend ought to be able to give us some information. My right hon. friend will remember with what exuberant language he spoke of the mission which this line was intended to accomplish, viewing it simply from a colonization point of view. How could my right hou. friend rise to those heights, without being able to say approximately the principal points, say within five or six hundred miles apart, which this line was intended to cover. In the province of Quebec they call this the Indian line, because like the Indian of old, to which my right hon. friend has referred, it passes far away from civilization, and that description seems to be verified by the statement of the Prime Minister. Of course, if he says it is impossible to give the committee any information on that point, I will not insist any further.

It seems to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) is a little inconsistent in his remarks this morning. The cry of most of the speakers on the other side has been that they wanted to give immediate relief to the settlers of the west.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) now says that the government must locate this line north of the Canadian Northern Railway, where there are practically no settlers at the present time. I take the ground that I took before the committee, that we should place no restrictions on any railway company going through the west. In this Bill at present we have the restriction that this road is to run south of Lake Abitibi and north of Lake Nepigon, and if you look at the map you will find that this limits it within a distance of 50 or 100 miles through the northern part of Ontario. Then, when they start out from that to Winnipeg, I do not suppose that they are going to run around in circles. After you get to Winnipeg the Bill says that the line shall run from there to Edmonton, and I submit that it ought to be left to the company and to the locating engineers as to which is the most available route.
I do not think this Bill says that the line is to run from Winnipeg to Edmonton.
It is so stated in their charter.
That is another Bill altogether.

I suppose they will have to stick to their charter or get it amended. I pointed out in the committee, that this 30 miles restriction would not work out in practice, and I am of that mind yet. Let me ask, whoever heard of a company taking a contract and signing it before they sent out their engineers ?
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen opposite laugh too soon. I mean to say that the proper course for the company to pursue would be to make some definite arrangement and then go to the expense of sending out their engineers. Look at what the Canadian Pacific Railway are doing to-day. Although the Canadian Pacific Railway has been in operation for twenty years they are making more changes on their line this year than they have in the last twenty years. They are changing the line from Winnipeg to Rat Portage and from Moosejaw to Swift Current and they are changing it at several places in the mountains. The Canadian Northern Railway now runs from Grandview to Saskatoon, but that is not the route that they at first intended to take. It was to have been built to the Pas on the Saskatchewan on its Hudson bay route, and it was intended to divert the line from a point on that line near the Pas Mission on the Saskatchewan west, via Prince Albert to Edmonton, which was to be its main line. The route to Grandview was never intended at first. There was merely a branch line built from Dauphin to Grandview, and they found by the extension of that branch line through that cut formed by the Duck mountains and the Riding mountains they would get a better main line than via Prince Albert. Ultimately they abandoned the Prince Albert line as the main line, and extended their Grandview branch, but they are nearly 150 miles apart at some points. It is the same way with this line which we are now discussing. I think the Grand Trunk Pacific should be allowed to locate their line where they can find the most traffic, wherever there is the best country, wherever they can get the most direct line, and wherever they can find the best roadbed. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) tells me that this is called the Indian line in the province of Quebec, but that would more appropriately apply to the Canadian Pacific Railway, because the Canadian Pacific Railway follows the old Indian trails almost directly across the prairies and through the mountains. In fact, their whole engineering feats in the mountains exactly follow up the old Cariboo trail located by the Indian. The switch backs that you see as laid out by the engineers of the Canadian Pacific Railway, can be found duplicated in certain places on the old Cariboo trail, notably at a point three or four miles south of the Elcho station on the Kootenay line. It was said by some gentlemen on the other side, that this new road should not be allowed to go near the existing lines of railway. Well, as I understand it. the people of the west are crying out for competing railways, so that they may have competition in freight rates. It is all very well to say that you are going to give us a trunk line, but should we not have competition in freight and passenger rates the same as you have in the east. If I go down to Montreal I can see

out of the car window another train running alongside of me for quite a distance. Are you in the east any better than we in the west, that you should have railways one mile apart, and that we should he compelled to have them 50 miles apart ?
Do you always get competition when the railways are alongside V

My experience is that we do. The Canadian Northern Railway gives us competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway as far as their line goes. While I criticised some time ago the action of Premier Roblin in aiding that road to parallel the Canadian Pacific Railway so closely, I see now that he was quite right in one way.
Hear, hear.

Yes, I have not said a word against him. I have not in this House or out of this House either said anything against that gentleman. He has subsidized this line to the extent of $10,000 or $15,000 a mile and it runs in some places only a mile apart from the Canadian Pacific Railway. The farmers have got the benefit of that, and the rate was cut at one time from 14 cents to 12 cents per hundred pounds and I believe it was cut yesterday to 10 cents per hundred pounds, which means a very material benefit to a large number of farmers in the west. I submit that the Grand Trunk Pacific should be allowed to build its main line or branches so as'to give the same competition to the other farmers of the west who wish to raise grain. It will be a great boon to them. I see no reason why the settlers in the west should not have just the same competition in passenger and freight rates as you have between Ottawa and Montreal or between Ottawa and Toronto.

The remarks just made by the hon. member (Mr. McCreary) seem to emphasize the point made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) as to the necessity of information being given to this committee before we can intelligently discuss this Bill. Here is an hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) who has listened to the discussion I presume for the last couple of weeks, who comes from the part of the country particularly interested and who, more than any other man in the House, would be supposed to hare obtained access to these mountains of information, and yet, he actually does'nt know this morning what Bill is before the House. He seemed to have a dream that it was the old Grand Trunk Pacific private Bill, and he did not even know that it is not provided in that Bill that the road should run from Winnipeg to Edmonton. In this present Bill he will find that the location is very open as regards the western division,' and that it merely says that it shall go through the provinces of Manitoba, and British Columbia, and the North-west Territories. The Mr. McCREARY.
government must see that if we are to be asked to vote intelligently on this question us to the aid we should give, that question will depend to a certain extent on the location of the road. If the road is to be of national benefit there must be localities in which it could be more properly constructed than within 30 or 31 miles of the Canadian Northern or of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Surely in a country hundreds of miles in width, nobody would feel more than the right hon. gentleman the folly of insisting that the company should be pinned down to keep within a certain distance of other roads. We have no desire to refuse legitimate assistance to this railway, but before we can say what aid should be given we should know at least within 100 miles of where this road is to be located. The same remark applies, with perhaps even more force, to the eastern end, for we do not even know whether it is to pass to the north or the south of the height of land. It would be unreasonable if we tried to pin the government down to ten miles or even twenty miles, but surely the government ought to be able to say within 100 miles of where this road is to be located.

Touching the observation of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that this is called the Indian line, because it is to go as far as possible from civilization, let me remind him that the last words of criticism we heard from hon. gentlemen opposite yesterday were, that the great fault of the scheme was that the line would not go further away from civilization and that the proper line would go very much farther north and away from civilization than any line that is possible under this contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
When I addressed the House on the project which we are now discussing, I expressed the desire that the right hon. gentleman would give us some'information on the very point which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has called attention to. We have already two lines of railway in the west. That was not the case when the Canadian Pacific Railway was initiated. We are face to face with an altogether new condition of affairs. The hon. Minister of the Interior stated to the House that the project that we are invited to approve would give an additional value of $3 or $4 an acre to 20,000,000 acres of land. That was one of his main points. We should be in a position to judge whether that statement was accurate or not. We have subsidized these two lines of railway. The right hon. gentleman has invited us not to give too much faith to rumours. I share bis views on that point. But there are rumours and rumours. There is a rumour to the effect that there might perhaps be some arrangement made by which one of the existing lines would be acquired ;

and there is a rumour that that line may he paralleled to a certain extent, in which case in the minds of certain people, there would be no hope for it to live. Everybody speaks of these rumours, and it is only fair, I think, that we should have some statement. But leaving that state of the case aside, let me remind the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, and parliament, of what the hon. Minister of the Interior stated, and stated truly. tie reminded us that to the south of the Canadian frontier there are American railways looking for the trade of the west, and he told us that unless we took great care our Canadian trade might go in that direction. The hon. Minister of the Interior invited us to give our attention to that point. Kindly look at the map of the Great Northern Railway, the Chicago, Burlington and Quin-cey Railway and the Northern Pacific Railway, which are just at our doors. Under these circumstances, is it not necessary for Us to insist that we should know where the location of the future line is to be? I invite my right hon. friend and his colleagues to look at this map, which I lay on the Table. These systems of American railways are competing against us; and are looking for the future trade. Let me place on the Table another map, which is of great importance, and which shows how necessary it is that we should be careful in such matters. The Canadian Northern Railway was located in the way we know. It runs partly through the state of Minnesota. Well', on the map of Mr. Hill's system of American railways, our rivals, there is shown a prospective line from the American frontier at Rainy lake to the American system of railways. It seems to me that we cannot be indifferent in a matter of this kind. I invite the attention of parliament, especially the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, to the great importance of telling the country, approximately, if they can, where the line that we ai-e subsidizing is going to be located.

The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), I think it was, spoke of the location of the Canadian Northern line. The original intention, as everybody knows, was to carry the Canadian Northern line to the Pas Mission. It was insisted upon by the Manitoba government that it should run there, and the assistance given to it was on that distinct condition. As the road developed, it transpired that it would be very advisable that that road should open up the territories towards Prince Albert, and the hon. member is correct in saying that the intention was that it should proceed on to Edmonton. It was found that, located as it was, it would be more or less of a winding road- that it would have to deviate either to the north or south from Prince Albert, and come into Edmonton either from a north-easterly or a south-easterly direction. Therefore, it was decided to have the main line located
as it is now; and it runs in almost an air line from Dauphin, south of the Duck mountains, across Saskatchewan, and on to Edmonton. There is no doubt that the people of this country would like to see this new line located so as to open up new territories to the north, instead of going through a country which, when the roads now under construction are completed, will be already well served. I am satisfied that the country would hesitate about giving a guarantee of bonds to two railways running over practically the same area and for the very same purpose. The Canadian Northern has a guarantee of $13,000 a mile, and if this road is to run over the same country, it is not necessary to guarantee its bonds. I remember distinctly that it was stated in this House that the Canadian Northern must give running rights to other roads. Why not let the Grand Trunk, then, use the Canadian Northern line as far as Edmonton, and as far as the government guarantee extends, until the needs of the country requires another transcontinental line beyond that point ? My hon. friend from St. Mary's division, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte), has pointed out another very important feature of til's Bill. From the outset, I have never believed, and I do not think that any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House who is cognizant of the facts of thS case believes for one second, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Company have any other object in view than to run via St. Paul and Minneapolis. Why should they ? The Grand Trunk Railway is in Chicago to-day, and it is in Minneapolis to-day. It may as well be understood that the Grand Trunk Railway Company controls and practically owns the Wisconsin Central Railway, which has its branches in Milwaukee and to Manitowoc on the west side of Lake Michigan, forty or fifty miles further north. The Grand Trunk Railway on the eastern side of Lake Michigan has a railway into Grand Rapids and to another port a few miles further north, the old Detroit, Grand Haven and Milwaukee system : and as the main line runs on to Duluth, all they have to do, once this Bill passes the committee, in order to have the best possible transcontinental line from the Atlantic to the Pacific that can possibly be selected, is to make an arrangement with J. J. Hill's company, and I am assured that they already have an understanding. Mr. Hill has two lines very nearly up to the Canadian border, along the Red river valley. These two lines connect with the wheat belt of the west and have branches into Duluth. He has a third line from the north into Duluth. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway do not wish to build, all they have to do is to make running arrangements with Mr. Hill, which he would gladly give, because he has these two other lines up the Red river valley within a stone's throw of each other.

and they run into Duluth and Minneapolis. The railway time from Toronto via Chicago to-day, according to the limited trains, compared with the Canadian Pacific Railway limited trains to Winnipeg, is forty-three minutes in favour of the Chicago route, so that you will readily understand that there are no great difficulties standing in the way of a route to the Canadian prairies via Chicago. And why should they not have it ? In giving the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway absolute ownership of the route west of Winnipeg, the government are carrying out the very thing they say they want to avoid. They makeitalmostobligatory on the Grand Trunk Railway to connect the Chicago and Minneapolis end with the Winnipeg end. Why should the Grand Trunk Railway carry coal thousands of miles away up in the northern region when they have their own route via Chicago ? Any other railway company, any independent company, controlled by agreement with the government, would be better than the Grand Trunk Railway to control this transcontinental road. I cannot see how any one can think that a man like Mr. Hays would haul his freight over a government road, in which he has no interest, when all he wants is a connecting link of 471 miles to bring his line to Minneapolis and a short branch therefrom to Duluth. 'The Grand Trunk Railway have the Central Vermont running down to New London and New York. It directly connects with Boston and Portland and Quebec and Montreal on the east. They go from Toronto through a fertile freight-producing country all the way via Chicago. They cross Michigan into Chicago and then draw from St. Louis and tap all the western states. They go into Minneapolis and have a branch to Milwaukee. Then they go to Winnipeg and onward through a broad fertile belt, then they pass through the Peace river pass on to the Pacific ocean. The Santa Fee road *is upwards of 3,500 miles from New York via Chicago to San Francisco. What about Manitoba ?

I believe that the only living Tory premier in Canada is opposing this scheme. But let me point out that many other premiers are supporting It, while hon. gentlemen opposite are opposing it. If my hon. friend thinks he can prove his argument by this one rare specimen of provincial government, which he has on the Conservative side, all we can say is that we admit the exception, but the Premier of Manitoba is not the only pebble on the beach. So it is a good thing for the maritime provinces and a good thing for Quebec. We are going to catch Ontario, the whole of the province of British Columbia is practically in favour of it, and the Tory agents in the territories are writing letters in favour of it. So that practically from ocean to ocean the people are supporting this scheme.
The children cry for it.

Yes, the children cry for it, and they are going to get it. I say that the hon. member for East York, who is very zealous in these matters, but possibly sometimes a little indiscreet, has acknowledged the whole thing now ; he has acknowledged that this scheme is supported by the public opinion of Canada. He uses the expression that we are going to catch the provinces.
For a while.

Yes, quite so. We do not expect to stay here until the end of the fifty years' term for Which we are dealing with this matter. We are not monopolists. This is a scheme in the public interest, and this government does not want a monopoly of office. We shall be quite willing to hold office for ten or fifteen years longer, and then give way to the new race of men who will come up in the opposition and will be capable of dealing with large and important questions. The hon. member for East York is a newspaper man, and whatever may be said by others about placing confidence in rumours circulated in the press, he should know better. There are people who assume, when they read something in a newspaper, that it is true. My hon. friend, if he reads his own paper, has reason to assume the opposite.
What about your own paper ? Are you judging me by yourself ?
My hon. friend asks what about my paper. I have lmd nothing to do with a paper for twenty years.
Were you found out V

I left I the newspaper business, and since I

left it and the hon. gentleman came into it, its reputation does not seem to have improved. However, no one knows better than my hon. friend the readiness with which newspaper correspondents imagine things and set rumours afloat ; and he knows that it would be utterly preposterous to take account in this House of the idle and silly rumours which the opposition newspapers print. Nobody knows that better than the hon. gentleman himself. He has referred to some rumours in reference to Senator Cox. He has referred to something stated in a newspaper, but I notice that my hon. friend did not quote or read it. However, I do not attach much importance to that. I take the substance of what he said. I understand that he referred to the relations of Senator Cox with this company. He said that the name of Senator Cox had been dropped out of the Bill. Well, he discovered that that was a mistake. The name has not been dropped [DOT] out of the Bill. Senator Cox appears, so far as we know, to have precisely the same relation to this contract that he had in the beginning. His name, with those of a number of other gentlemen, was placed in the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill, and it is still there. What Senator Cox's relations with that company may be we know nothing and care nothing. These gentlemen, as members of a corporation, stand precisely on the same footing as others who may be members of a corporation, and we know no more than the hon. gentleman himself, as to whether Senator Cox is to remain in the company or go out of it. That is his own and the company's business, and we have nothing to do with it. By my hon. friend went further. He said that there must be large flotations of money by the government in connection with this great "transaction, and that there were rumours in the Toronto ' Star,' a paper favourable to the government, that in connection with these large flotations of government loans, Senator Cox was to have his share of the profits or was to have something to do with them. Am I correct ? I have stated it correctly, as the hon. gentleman stated it. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that there is not and never has been a shadow of foundation for anything of the kind ; that Senator Cox has never been in any way associated with any question touching the action of the government in connection with the flotation of loans in this matter ; and that the large sums of money which it may be necessary to raise to carry out this enterprise, so far as the government is concerned, will be raised in the ordinary way, by the Minister of Finance, in the great money markets of the world, or through the banks of Canada. by open, public tender and contract with the man who is prepared to supply the money on the most favourable terms.

I must confess that I am a little surprised at the Finance Minister. This question arose, as I understand it, by the hon. leader of the opposition asking for information as to where this railroad is going to be located. Now, what information have we got from the minister ? The Minister of Justice told us that they were aware that the American railroads were approaching the territory of Manitoba, and that the government were going to see that they did not accomplish the object they have in view ; but I did not understand him to say what he was going to do to prevent the traffic of Manitoba and the North-west drifting down into the United States. All he told us was that the government had the power in their hands to prevent it, and that they were going to do so. We must vote it blind, and let the government, after the surveys are made, say where the location of this line is to be. Then, we have the Finance Minister jumping on his feet and making a backwoods stump speech. I was much surprised to hear the Finance Minister of Canada make such a speech in this House on this important question. To my mind it is beneath the dignity of the Finance Minister of Canada. With all respect to the right hon. leader of this House, I think the opposition are entitled to information before we vote this large sum of money. I recollect very well, when I had the honour of sitting on the government side of the House with the present gentlemen in that the right hon. leader of the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce used to object very strongly to placing too much power in the hands of the government, to be exercised beyond the control of the House. They contended-and I felt that there was some truth in their position-that the House should have something to say in reference to the location of railway lines and the expenditure of public money. But they have gone back on that proposition just as they have gone back on all the propositions that they ever submitted to this House and the country. Now they tell us that we must vote it blind, that we must have faith in them, seeing that the trade of the North-west does not go to the United States. I see my right hon. friend smiling.
My hon. friend says I have gone back on my former principles. I think my hon. friend has gone back also.

No, I am going forward, but you have gone back on everything you told this House when in opposition. I challenge you to name one principle that you advocated in opposition that you have carried out, and I challenge the electors of East Northumberland to say that 1 have ever gone back on one pledge I ever
