made to the electors. Although I have a good deal of confidence in the hon. Minister of Justice, I have not enough confidence in the men he is surrounded by to trust a great franchise to them.
At one o'clock, Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

This morning I took the liberty of drawing the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that in my opinion the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway has no intention whatever of utilizing the line north of Lake Superior. And as supporting that view, I would ask permission to quote from the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' its report of a meeting held in the city of Minneapolis. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) was on a visit to the western and north-western states and was tendered a banquet by the citizens of Minneapolis. At that banquet, Mr. J. J. Hill, President of the Great Northern Railway presided, and in the course of his remarks said :
The spirit largely predominated too, that the man they were honouring was willing to meet them half way in any business proposition they were in a position to make. That feeling of the gathering was put into words by President J. J. Hill, of the Great Northern Railway, who delivered the address of welcome. Many excellent vocal numbers were given by the Orpheus quartette.
In his address Mi. Hill said :
If we had any cause to find fault, it would be well for us to cultivate their good graces, but fortunately there is no necessity for doing so. One of the strongest ties, that bind us is our mutual trade relations, and the fact that we use the same great natural highway, the St. Lawrence river.
In this connection I might say that the people ojf Minneapolis; evidently do not regard the abrogation of the bonding privilege as any menace to the people of Canada, but rather to the people of the western states.
If this channel would be improved it could carry the commerce of the northern States and Canada. It would carry the great bulk of our products if it were properly improved. One of the greatest considerations in favour of reciprocal relations between Canada and our own country is that we understand each other. In order to trade successfully with customers we must look for one where we can collect the debt. We may be always certain of our pay when dealing with our northern neighbours, for we know that their laws will be enforced. This question of getting our pay is what distinguishes our trade relations with Canada from those with countries where we cannot collect our claims.
. . . The exports of Great Britain are five times our per capita, and even Canada with her six million people, exports twice as much per capita as we do. If we merely exchange our products among ourselves we are not richer as a nation, but if we put our goods in foreign markets, the value of our exports represents profit.
The fact that the United States exported some odd millions to Canada more than Canada did to the United States represents the profit which the Americans made out of us according to Mr. Hill.
He has just told you that we export more than they do.

Per capita. But he did not tell us that the manufacturing industries in the great commercial centres of the United States, built up under their national policy, consumed the major portion and it is only their surplus that they export to Canada.
Canada exports more per capita.

Because we have not sufficient consumers at home. Our object is to export less and consume more at home, but Mr. Hill is looking for a new market to which they can export the surplus products of the United States, which represents their profit. He goes on to say :
If we do not change our attitude we will have to have a fence to keep our people in.
All this shows that the people of Minnesota are anxious to capture the trade of our Canadian North-west. Then I find this very striking sentence in the speech of the Minister of the Interior :
The essential thing about a people is virtue, and having that they will be able to carry out their ends and designs without any difficulty.
. . . The effort to form a reciprocity treaty a few years ago when the commission met in Washington failed, in my judgement, because there was lacking a determination and spirit for mutual concessions and compromises. If you will look up the definition of the word ' reciprocity ' you will find that it does not apply to such a state of feeling. Whether another attempt to formulate a treaty will meet with better success depends largely upon the people of the United States. I will say that Canada will make no treaty under the terms of which she will not get as much as she gives. It appears to me that the sentiment in favour of the formation of a reciprocity treaty is growing in the United States, but as yet a small proportion of the country has expressed its opinion. The government must act, however, upon the desires of the majority of the people.
He went on to show how the American people must influence their state legislatures and congress to bring that about. Upwards of four hundred of the leading business men of Minneapolis and St. Paul were at that meeting. On that same day, the 12th of January, 1903, I find a map in the ' Winnipeg Free Press ' headed ' the roa d the pro- ' vince lost,' and I find that the ' Free Press,' Mr. Sifton's paper, found fault with the government of Mr. Roblin for having refused a charter to a railway company to cross the American boundary line from the state of Minnesota at four different points. About

the same time, we find a renewal of the application to cross at four points from Minnesota and Dakota into the province of Manitoba, and three of these lines would extend westward into the territories. There can be no doubt that this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway scheme is associated with the identical proposition emanating from Minneapolis and St. Paul, and it is very strange indeed that, following so soon after this meeting, we find this application to the legislature of Manitoba for these lines to cross the border at four different points from Dakota and Minnesota and then cross the wheat fields and tap Saskatchewan and Assiniboia at three points, and on to Edmonton. Senator Cox had previously had communication with these gentlemen and devised with them this great plan to open up the prairies of the North-west. What I claim is that the members of this House and the people of this country are entitled to know what data the government have. Have they any data to give this House in relation to the plans arranged by this Grand Trunk Pacific Company with Mr. J. J. Hill and the Wisconsin Central or any other American road, and their plans with relation to entering the harbour of Duluth ?

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) a question ? Are we to understand from the tenor of his remarks that Mr. Goblin's government last session granted a charter to American lines to touch the four places mentioned by him and subsidized that line to the extent of $3,570,000. And does he mean to say that this was done at the instance of the Minister of the Interior, and that the Minister of the Interior has such influence with the Roblin government as to cause it thus to assist the Grand Trunk ? Practically that is what he said.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) was up rather late last night, like the rest of us. I hope he got home in a satisfactory condition. But, certainly, to use the common expression, be is talking through his hat now. I have said that this article was headed 1 The Road the Province Lost,' that shows that the Manitoba government did not subsidize
They did.
Nothing of the kind.
They bonused them this session, and the hon. gentleman said so a moment ago.
The Manitoba government declined to pass the charter, last year knowing that it was not in the interest of the country.
Well, I leave it to the other hon. members for Manitoba.

Having pledged the credit of the province of Manitoba to develop the province and to provide the farmers with the facilities for getting their products to market quickly and readily, it is not likely that they are going to tax the people of that province to build up Duluth and other American centres.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to consult his friends from Marquette (Mr. Roche), Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) and Provencher (Mr. LaRiviere) whether they passed that charter or not.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) to say that they subsidized this road ?
Yes, to the extent of $3,570,000, passed on the very last day of the session; and it is on record.

Not one dollar was voted by the legislature of Manitoba for this road or any similar road. But I think the country is entitled to some statement as to this line. I am not opposing a line by the states. It is a profitable line for the Grand Trunk to take. When they came forward and said they were going to build a line north of the lakes, everybody knew there was deception in it somewhere, and that it was only intended to tickle the fancy of those whose motive is to pose as Canadian patriots. I would like to know why this line from Winnipeg to the west will be the absolute property of the Grand Trunk instead of the property of the government? Why are they not compelled to own the line east of Winnipeg and the government line west Of Winnipeg ?
I have answered these questions again and again during the debate. The question put by my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) is not new, but has been answered many times.
The Prime Minister, I take it, understands that the, Grand Trunk intends running their main traffic to the sea-board through American channels.

That is not the question the hon. gentleman asked. His question was why the Grand Trunk were allowed to build the line west of Winnipeg instead of the government. I told him that the answer to that question had been given again and again during the debate.
I never heard it.
If the hon. gentleman did not hear it, I am sorry for his understanding.
I heard an excuse or two, but no reason.

Another question he has asked me, I thought he did not insist upon, but I see that he wants infor-

mation. He asks wliat is the arrangement between the Grand Trunk and Mr. j. J. Hill for carrying the whole system into the North-west. I do not know that there is any such arrangement; I never heard of it, and I do not believe it.

The hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) makes the assertion that the Grand. Trunk Company, by acquiring the Wisconsin Central and reaching Minneapolis, show a design to carry its traffic from the North-west through American channels. I think the inference drawn by the hon. gentleman is entirely unwarranted. I would point out to the hon. gentleman that the transcontinental line we now have, the Canadian Pacific Railway, has a railway to Minneapolis, and also controls a railway line from Mineapolis to our North-west, joining the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Moosejaw. For reasons quite satisfactory to themselves, that company desired this American connection. At the time the Canadian Pacific Railway acquired the road from Sauit Ste. Marie to Minneapolis and from Sauit Ste. Marie to Duluth, the Grand Trunk, under the management of the board in England, failed to secure one of these lines, as it ought to have done. Since that time, the Grand Trunk has been labouring under a serious disadvantage with regard to traffic originating at Minneapolis and at other Minnesota and North-west points. The Grand Trunk Company has now', and for many years has had, a line from Port Huron to Chicago. It competes for western trade over that line. It carries a large amount of western freight to Montreal, while a large amount it diverts from the channels it would naturally follow to New' York, Philadelphia and Baltimore, and sends a large amount of this American trade to Portland that does not go to Montreal. Now, by acquiring the Wisconsin Central and securing the line to Minneapolis, the Grand Trunk Company simply places itself in the same position that the Canadian Pacific Railway occupied and has occupied for years, in a position where it can compete at Minneapolis and Minnesota for business going to the New England states, of which trade the Canadian Pacific Railway, at the present moment, to a large extent, has the monopoly. So far as drawing trade from the Canadian North-west by that route to the sea is concerned, the Canadian Pacific Railway is in a position to take trade by that route to-day, having the connections I have stated. in the future, it is highly probable that there will be a large amount of wheat purchased in the North-west for milling and consumption in the United States and the Canadian Pacific Railway is in a position to furnish facilities for transaction of that trade. If the Grand Trunk chooses to push this line beyond Minneapolis and into the North-west, it takes a step to
place .itself in the position similar to the one occupied by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
How would the Canadian Pacific Railway bring trade to Minneapolis ?

From Moosejaw; from a very rich wheat-growing region. Or it can bring this grain from Winnipeg by the line to Pembina. It has two lines by which it can reach Minneapolis from the Northwest. It is perfectly absurd to make the assertion here that the Grand Trunk Company, in seeking to place itself in the same position as is occupied by the Canadian Pacific Railway, is laying a plan to divert trade from our own seaports to American ports. There is no probability whatever that the Grand Trunk Company will carry grain by way of Minneapolis and Chicago all-rail to the sea-board.
How does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) suggest they will haul it until the eastern section is built ?

The probability is that they will have connection with Lake Superior or some port upon that lake, and they will deliver wheat there for transmission to the sea-board by that route. But so far as the all-rail route is concerned, when the line is built from Quebec to Winnipeg on the route laid down at present, no other line from the North-west to the sea-board is in it at all.
How does the hon. gentleman propose that the Grand Trunk shall get to Port Arthur ?

I shall advise the Grand Trunk to keep away from Port Arthur, I shall advise the managers of the Grand Trunk to run a line from their main line, from their transcontinental line which passes north of Lake Nepigon, to Nepigon bay. where they will have a better harbour, where they will be nearer the foot of Lake Superior, and which they can reach by better grades and by a better road than the route to Port Arthur. It is not necessary to go to Port Arthur, it is not advisable to go to Port Arthur, in connection with this scheme for building a road from Quebec to Winnipeg.
How would a line to Duluth do ?

That is the line that my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, is attached to. It may possibly be that the Grand Trunk, in the meantime, before the line is constructed from Quebec to Winnipeg, a branch line from that main line to Nepigon bay-it may be that the Grand Trunk will be obliged to avail itself of other modes of egress, it may possibly have to seek egress at Port Arthur, It may possibly have to reach Duluth. But when this scheme is completed, when the line is

built from Quebec to Winnipeg and extended on to the Pacific ocean, then the natural result -will be that the Grand Trunk will have a branch to Nepigon bay, and will be independent of all other lines, and can lay its wheat down either at Quebec or at a port upon Lake Superior, at Nepigon, to greater advantage and cheaper than any other line engaged in the transportation of the products of the Canadian North-west can do it.
By what authority does the hon. gentleman suggest the Nepigon bay line ? Has he any authority from Senator Cox and the Grand Trunk ?

I have not. I assume that the Grand Trunk Company will have a connection with Lake Superior from the main line. I am justified in making this assumption, because such has been stated to be the case. I assume that the Grand Trunk Company will seek the best harbour and by the shortest branch line that they can command, and that will be from the main line west of Lake Nepigon to Nepigon harbour upon Lake Superior ?
Does not the hon. gentleman know that they have already taken powers in their charter to build a branch to Port Arthur, and not to Nepigon ?

Well, it does not matter what they have, taken powers to do, and if they should choose to build a line to Port Arthur, a line which will be longer than one to Nepigon and which will not serve their purpose as well, they nevertheless are reaching Lake Superior. It will be for them to decide what they will do. I The charter, I understand, has been amend-1 ed in the Senate and provision has been made I that they shall go to Nepigon bay, an obvious course to pursue. Now, Sir, with regard to the contention that was raised when we first commenced the discussion of clause 2 by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, that we should have definite information a? to the location of this line, that we were not justified in proceeding to make a contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, that the people of the country ought not to justify the action the government are taking until everything was known about this line, until the line was surveyed and located, and we knew exactly what the character of the country was, knew the exact points it would touch in the route between Quebec and Port Simpson or Bute Inlet well, I think this contention is an absurd one. When the Canadian Pacific Railway was chartered, Callender was named as one of the termini and the Pacific ocean as the other. Nothing was known as to the intermediate route of that road. The fact is that the surveys that were made by the Mackenzie government called for a route along the Saskatchewan river and

through the Yellow Head pass, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company took an entirely different route from Winnipeg west, one through the Kicking Horse pass, by the Columbia river and over the Rogers' pass in the Selkirk range, and north-west of the Columbia down to Revelstoke, through the mountains and down the Thompson canyon, and never touched the line that was surveyed and was designed to be pursued from Winnipeg west, until they had crossed the prairies and crossed the mountains and reached the junction of the Thompson river and the Fraser river in British Columbia. With regard to the Canadian Northern Railway, we have granted aid to that line without knowing exactly where it was to be located, granted that aid in advance of the location of the line.
When ?
I prefer to finish my remarks now.

Will the hon. member tell us what aid was granted to that line in advance of the surveys ? Nothing of the kind was done. The surveys were registered in the Department of Railways and Canals for that road long before that charter passed this House.
Mr. MeOREARY. They got a land grant and a subsidy to go to Hudson's bay, but there has never been a survey made of the road so far as I know.
That Is the Hudson's bay road.
It is the Canadian Northern.
It is nothiug of the kind.
What difference does the name make anyway ?

Now, with regard to the contention that these surveys ought to have been made, that we ought'not to proceed to make these preliminary arrangements until we knew exactly where this line was going, what the course would be, and everything in connection with the line, with the information that will be furnished by a thorough and exhaustive survey-well,
I say that course has not been pursued hitherto with regard to transcontinental lines. I say furthermore that that course was unnecessary. Here are certain salient points that stand out in this case. In the first place, we have an enormous region in the North-west which is rapidly settling, thousands of settlers are pouring into that country. There is reason to believe, before five years have elapsed, the productions of that country will have more than doubled. We know that that country is sadly in need of railway communication, of means of getting its productions to market. We know that

these cannot be furnished immediately, that it is a work of time. We know furthermore that the loss, even of a year, in making the preparations -which are essentially necessary, would prove to be a most serious matter before this road was ready for business. Now, the government were confronted with these conditions, with the imperative necessity of providing transportation facilities for a region of enormous extent and of untold resources and capabilities, a region that we know will settle up with great rapidity. Confronted with these conditions the question for the government to decide was this :	Can we proceed to
make arrangements for giving to that country an outlet by rail, and can we proceed to make these arrangements now and do it safely ? Well, here was a proposition, first of all, to build a road upon Canadian soil. That is one point laid down which would confine the government in the location of this road within certain limits. They were to build the road from ocean to ocean on, Canadian soil. Does any hon. gentleman object to that ? Then our most natural, our only actual sea-port to start from on the Atlantic coast, was Quebec. Now, the question that arose was this, if we start from Quebec where shall we aim for ?, Shall we go north of Lake Winnipeg by the Trans-Canada project ? What shall we aim at as the point of concentration for the business of the North-west where all that business is poured into one common receptacle ? Shall we aim for Winnipeg ? I think we wisely decided to aim for Winnipeg. Well, here were two points fixed. Then Winnipeg being midway between the eastern terminus and the Pacific ocean
Where is the eastern terminus placed ?
At Quebec.

Where did you say ?
Mr. CiHARLTON. At Quebec. Then, Mr. Chairman, the next question was : What can we probably do in the matter of the location of the route between Quebec and Winnipeg ? We are told by our hon. friends opposite that the information we have of that country is of the most hazy, indefinite and unreliable character. I deny it. We have information with regard to this country of a tolerably definite and reliable character. We actually had one railway line run north of Lake Nepigon, from the head of Montreal river, substantially upon the line that this road will follow. We had an instrumental survey, practically, of the western half of the division from Quebec to Winnipeg. Then we have had explorations of the whole of that region. It cannot perhaps be said that every square mile has been visited, but explorations of sufficient minuteness have been made to give us reliable information as to the
general character of the country and to give a general idea as to the character of the line on which this road will be located, and from these we know that we can secure a highly favourable line. I predict that we can secure a line from Quebec to Winnipeg -possibly with the exception of the Lauren-tian range- with grades not exceeding four-tenths per cent to the mile, and I believe that within a few months will have information which will confirm that prediction.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman what reports that have been laid on the Table will show that ?

My hon. friend wants to know what reports show that. This road will pass through the great alluvial region south of James bay. It passes through a level country with slight elevations, a country favourable for railway construction, and I hazard the observation that there will be no difficulty in getting grades throughout that whole section of less than one half per cent.
That is a pure speculation.

It is not pure speculation, because we know the general character of the country from the height of land towards James bay. It is generally level in character, there is a vast amount of agricultural land in it, and we know that at Moose Factory, on the James bay, the mean summer temperature is one degree higher than at Winnipeg. We know also that there is a vast region there likely to be quite as productive as the valley of Lake St. John. The government had all of that information; they knew where they wanted to start this road and the points between which they wanted it to run. They knew the general character of the country, and they had an opportunity to make such a contract for the construction of this road as might not, be possible a year hence. They had an opportunity-
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) laughs. They had an opportunity to make arrangements for the construction of this road, and I think they showed great wisdom in at once seizing that opportunity. By it they will get a line of railway from Moncton to Bute Inlet or Port Simpson for an actual expenditure of money of not more than ip 15,000,000.
Oh, oh.

Yes, while the Canadian Pacific Railway cost this countrytaking land at its value to-day-$135,000,000 for the construction of 1,904 miles. That is deducting the line between Callender and Port Moody, the 645 miles which the govern-

ment constructed and handed over to the company.
This being the case, knowing the character of tile country, knowing the necessity of having a further outlet for the products of the west, knowing we could get a route of a favourable character-how favourable we do not know, nor do we know the exact percentage of good land-the government were wise in making this contract. We wanted that road primarily not for the local business that would originate along the line, but for the carrying of the grain and the multiform productions of the west to market, and by this contract we get a road that will serve that purpose.
Does any one doubt that from Winnipeg west a suitable route can be got to Bute Inlet or Port Simpson by way of the Peace river valley ?

Before the hon. gentleman leaves the eastern section might I ask him a question ? He has told us that an instrumental survey of one half the route of the eastern section has been made. May I ask him if he knows why that survey has not been laid on the Table of the House ?
I may tell my hon. friend that some years ago unfortunately a fire took place in Ottawa.
Oh, oh.

Yes, and the notes of this survey and all the information of a detailed character in connection with it were burned. For that reason we have none of this information available except the abstract report of Sir Sandford Fleming.
How does the hon. gentleman then know anything about what the report contained ?

I say we have the abstract report of Sir Sandford Fleming. Years ago a line was partially surveyed from Montreal to Winnipeg running north of Lake Nepigon, and it was found that a road could be constructed there with grades not exceeding 50 feet in the mile, and there were very few of these. It was also found that the rivers would not require bridging of over 300 feet in length. We have access to that information, but we have not the details.
The hon. gentleman says there will be grades of 50 feet to the mile ; that is double the grade which he asks for in this new line.

I do not say it is not possible to reduce a 50-foot grade to 25 feet by digging 25 feet. At that time, 25 years ago it was thought that a 50-foot grade was a very good one, but if with a road going through a favourable country a survey gives you grades of 50 feet per mile, I would say that to-day the same com-
pany, by spending some money, could reduce that grade to four-tenths per cent, or 21 feet per mile.
By spending money enough you could.

Exactly ; it is a question of money, and it is a desirable expenditure of money, because it increases the capacity of the road and it makes the road an earner of money, able to compete with other roads where without the expenditure of that money it might not serve that purpose at all.
I repeat then, that we had a general knowledge of this country sufficient to justify the government in making this arrangement if other circumstances seemed to warrant their doing so. The other circumstances were the opportunity to make a highly advantageous agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, an arrangement which if times were to change I do not believe we could make twelve months hence, an arrangement surprisingly favourable to the country and to the government, which, when carried to completion, will settle the transportation problem.
We are haggling here over these matters in a manner that I think a few months hence some hon. members engaged in this discussion will regret. I suppose that it is a legitimate thing to make party capital out of a government scheme, but it strikes me the opposition are adopting unfair tactics which I do not believe are to their advantage or to the advantage of the country.
The opposition will take care of themselves.

Of course they will, they have put their foot in it now up to the knee; they have opposed a project which the country will endorse ; they have taken just the kind of care of themselves that we like to see them take.
I may summarize by saying that I think the government were justified In deciding to enter into this arrangement and making this contract which was so advantageous that they could not afford to let it pass. They have gained a year by proceeding with the inception of a scheme designed to give transportation facilities to the Northwest, and by the time this road is completed the wisdom of their course will be made manifest by the crying necessity that will exist in the west for improved transportation facilities.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman for how much less per mile he expects this Grand Trunk Pacific Road will be able to carry grain to the eastern sea-board than the existing roads ?

I have some information on that point which I have elaborated, and will give more fully later on, but I may say now that I expect the Grand Trunk Pacific will carry wheat from Win-

nipeg to Quebec for 3 cents a bushel less than it is carried to-day by part rail and part water, by rail to Port Arthur, and thence by water to Montreal. I will prove that this is the case in due time. This road is going to solve the transportation problem and carry wheat from the Northwest Territories to the sea-board cheaper than it can be carried by any other line. Railway men have for two or three years past asserted that water transportation could not compete with railways having grades of four-tenths per cent, or 21 feet to the mile. Then it seemed to me that this assertion was absurd, but I believe, after full investigation of the data, that it is well founded, and I shall show in due time why I believe so.

As the hon. gentleman has taken a prominent part in this debate, will he state, on his reputation as a member of this House, that such a road as he speaks of can be built for $25,500 per mile through the country he has been describing ?
Which country is that?
North of Lake Superior.
1 never have asserted it could be built for that.
What is your guess ?
The estimate made by me for the construction of the road is very much higher-the guessing has been done on the other side.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) speaks of the opposition haggling over this matter, and he says we might be sorry later on for what we may say. There is no danger, however, that the opposition will be as inconsistent in their haggling as is the hon. gentleman. I draw his attention to the fact that during the discussion on the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill,
I remember him rising up in the committee and using this language-:
I don't believe in saddling 500 or 600 miles on the Grand Trunk Pacific to make a connection at Moncton to compete with the government railway thus making our own property valueless.
Who said that V
Name. Name.
Why, that was said by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who was put up in this House to defend the government scheme.
Surely you are mistaken.
No, and I would advise the government, that any time they have an atrociously inconsistent proposition to offer to this House, they should call on the member for North Norfolk to bolster it up.

I must interrupt my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram). I suppose I am bound
to accept the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram), but much as I admire him, I cannot believe that the hon. gentleman from North Norfolk made that statement. I must refuse to believe it until I hear from the lips of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) whether he has been correctly reported.
I do not very often address this House, and I do not wish to be interrupted.
Give him a chance to deny it.
Certainly, let him deny it if he can. But he cannot deny it, because on June 3rd, the member for North Norfolk used these very words in the committee and I took down his own words.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) will refer me to the page in ' Hansard ' we will have an authoritative statement as to whether it was said or not.
Oh.
There is no ' Hansard ' in the Railway Committee.
I suppose there is only one animal that never modifies its opinions, and that the jackass.
' Modifies ' is a good word.

Where a man is investigating a subject and investigates it carefully, he may secure facts and data that will prove to him that lie possibly sometime before that entertained erroneous opinions. I notice a very singular tendency on the part of friends on the opposite side of the House to branch off from the discussion of the merits of the case, and to try to prove that some have been guilty of inconsistency who some years ago may have entertained opinions that they do not entertain now. Where these hon. gentlemen find an instance of that kind, they seem to imagine that their case has been proved. Now, with regard to what I may have said about the Intercolonial Railway and the building of the short line, I would not deny ,to-day that I did believe at one time that it would be unnecessary and impolitic to parallel the Intercolonial Railway, and I presume that I have made statements to that effect. But, when we come to the consideration of a great transcontinental railway line scheme, and when it becomes apparent after investigating all the conditions relating to that scheme, that its success or failure depended on the work which should be done by it; when it becomes apparent that if we are to give business in the winter to the maritime province ports we must have the very best tools and the very best conditions; and when it becomes apparent that to send freight around a circuitous route with heavy grades, over the Intercolonial Railway, would put

us in a position where we could not realize the object we sought; then these conditions confronting one, one would naturally modify his opinions. Now, Sir, the question is not whether I once thought it would be impolitic to parallel the Intercolonial Railway and shorten this distance and lower these grades, but the question is, that we are building a transcontinental route from ocean to ocean, that we are seeking to place our own products at our own sea-ports and control our own trade, that we are carefully deliberating as to the methods and the means that are necessary to reach that desirable consummation, and if I make up my mind that the straightening of the Intercolonial, and the lowering of its grades were necessary in order to enable the Intercolonial Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific to compete with the New York Central, and the Pennsylvania, and other railways in the United States for the business of carrying wheat from the North-west to the sea-board, why, Sir, I will go back on any impression I may have formed before, and, judging from the data I have at my hand, and the investigations I am enabled to make, I will go for what I believe to be essentia] to the consummation of the project before me.
The hon. gentleman has probably satisfied himself by his explanation, but I do not think he has satisfied any other hon. gentleman in this House
I do not think I have satisfied you.

At the very time that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) used the words I have quoted we were considering the question of a transcontinental route. I do not wish that the hon. gentleman should say anything against the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but I would like to know from him why he should load up the government and the people of this country with a line that he refused to load on to the Giand Trunk Railway. If the hon. gentleman was not considering a transcontinental route in the committee, what was he considering ?
Anything in sight.
Yes, and if the argument on which he based that statement in the committee is sound, how does he proclaim it to be unsound within so short an interval ?
I have to say that 1 have very grave doubts about the accuracy of my hon. friend's statement.

Oh, if there is any doubt about that, it is only an instance of one inconsistency, and I can quote another one to show that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) is not logical. The hon. gentleman was giving reasons why the government should not state more in this Bill than the mere terminal points to which the Grand Trunk

Pacific Railway should run, and he said that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed there were only certain terminal points mentioned in the Bill. He thought that the same should be the case with the Grand Trunk Pacific. Does the hon. gentleman not know that circumstances and conditions have changed ? Does be not know that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built we had no railways in the North-west, and no settlement to give trade to a railway ? The people of this country were glad to get the Canadian Pacific Railway into that territory, and that is why they did not specify anything more than the terminal points.
Does the hon. gentleman say that we did not know anything about that western country before the Canadian Pacific Railway went into it ?

I did not say anything of the kind, because I know that we had much more information about the Canadian Pacific Railway and the country through which it was to pass, than we have with regard to this government scheme. What I am pointing out is that now, not only have we railways in the North-west but we have a. Iai'ge population there, and there is not that same necessity for a railway to-dav as there was then.

INGRAM- The hon. gentleman talks about the necessity being worse. Why, from the southern boundary of Manitoba to Lake Manitoba, they have now some ten railways, branches and main lines. And vet the hon. gentleman talks about the situation being worse than ever. It is ridiculous. When the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill was before the committee we were told that instead of uselessly wasting the time of the committee from day to day in discussing the assistance that was to be given by the government, that we should not mingle up that question with the Bill then before us [DOT] that we were simply called upon to vote lor a charter granting the Grand Trunk Pacific certain rights, and that the Grand Trunk Pacific had a perfect right to construct their line of railway wherever they liked so long as they paid for it. We were toidl by the Finance Minister and others speaking for the government that when the question of a subsidy or of assistance to the Grand Trunk Pacific came before the House, the government would be in a position to state where the road was to go What are we told to-day ? When I rise in my place and ask the question of the Minister of Justice, a gentleman whom I have hitherto always found very courteous in his replies, he snubs me by saying that he is not going to waste his time in answering paltry questions of that kind. I want to ask the government, is it not due to us and

to tlie people of this country that we should have some idea of where the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is going to run between the points named in the charter ? Ever since these hon. gentlemen assumed power the transportation question has occupied a large part of the time of this House from session to session. When the Grand Trunk Railway Company gave notice that they were going to ask for legislation from this parliament, they did not state their intention of constructing any portion of the line east of North Bay. That has been loaded on to them since. X believe it would have been in the interest of this country to have granted the company the right to build a line of railway from North Bay to the North-west, and to have granted them reasonable assistance for that purpose; but when the government insists on their building a line of railway which, as the hon. member for North Norfolk has stated, will interfere with the value of a government line already constructed, then they are going entirely beyond what I believe the people of this country will approve of. As I have stated, this great transcontinental question lias for years been discussed in this House, and I want to know from the leader of the government what his government have been doing for the last seven years towards relieving the congestion in the North-west ? Why did they not have surveyors out through the country locating a line ? Had they done that, instead of the opposition having to devote weeks in this House in the effort to obtain from the government information as to where this railway is to be located, the Prime Minister would have been in a position to say to railway contractors that the government were ready to build a line from a certain point to a certain point, and that the contract would be awarded to the lowest tenderer. He would have been in a position to give the very information which the opposition desire today. That would have been an intelligent course to pursue. But what is the position of the government to-day ? On one occasion, when there were eight ministers in their places, they were asked to state within $10,000,000 what this road would cost, and not a single answer came from them. I asked the Minister of Justice to-day if the government are going to reserve to themselves the right to say to the Grand Trunk Pacific, when they come to them with surveys, that unless the location suits them, they will refuse the aid. If they refuse the aid. what will become of this contract ? Considerable time must elapse before the surveys are presented to the government. Then, when any of the followers of the government go to the country and tell the people of the different provinces that the government are going to construct this line of railway from such a point to such a point, how will these hon. gentlemen know ? Not one of them, from the leader down, knows
where this road is to be built; and if they are going to the country, as it is reported they are, not one of them will be in a position to say where the road will be located ; and any argument they use along that line will be frustrated by the question, where is your authority for making the statement 1 You have none. The hon. Minister of Finance, to-day picked up the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), and said that the government, when they went to the country, would be in a. position to carry each province ; but he is not in a position to make his argument very effective unless he can state the location of this line of railway. The hon. member for North Norfolk said that we could secure the very perfect grade that he has spoken of by the expenditure of money. I want to tell my hon. friend that one of the best railway experts of the Dominion of Canada, who knows the territory in New Brunswick better, I presume, than any other man in the Dominion, told me that he would challenge any government or party to secure six expert railway engineers, and if one out of the six would state that the government would secure grades of the description named by the hon. member for North Norfolk, he would state something that was entirely impossible. From what I can learn of that country, I say it is simply impracticable to secure gradients through it of the character named by the hon. member for North Norfolk. Then, we have hon. gentlemen on the government side stating that a few miles of distance more or less do not enter into consideration in these long hauls ; but unless you have better grades, you gain no material advantage. The right hon. leader of the House stated that the through-line would be shortened 120 miles by building this railway in New Brunswick. This, under ordinary circumstances, would be of very material advantage ; but in view of the statement made by this expert, it would be impossible to secure grades that would give the new line any material advantage. X would suggest to the right hon. gentleman that instead of adopting that scheme at all, he had better improve the gradients on the Intercolonial Railway, and thus save the $70,000,000 of public money that has been put into that road, and extend the line, as the leader of the opposition suggested, to the Georgian bay. If he does that, I am sure he will not be sorry for it in the long run, and it will serve the people of this country much better than the scheme before the House. Had it not been for the political influence that was brought to bear upon the right hon. gentleman I doubt very much whether any such proposition wouid ever have been submitted to this House. I cannot believe that the right hon. gentleman, with his long experience, would contend for a moment that the construction of this line, as proposed, is in the best interests of the people. I can only conclude that he was

compelled to give his assent to this scheme by the strong pressure of his political supporters, who have an eye to their own reelection rather than the building of a proper transcontinental line. My attention has been drawn to a statement which appeared In the ' Globe ' of June 4th, 1903, and I wouldi ask the attention of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) to this paper, which he is in the habit of quoting himself pretty often :
Mr. John Charlton protested against having the Grand Trunk Railway saddled with con-, ditions which would make the road an unprofitable undertaking. He favoured Mr. McCreary's suggestion and thought that if Quebec could be kept open by navigation all winter the road should be allowed to be built from Quebec to Winnipeg.
But he was down on the extension from Quebec to Moncton.

a question arose a moment ago with reference to a statement made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes). I understood him to say that a certain charter had been asked for from the Manitoba government shortly after the visit of the Minister of the Interior to St. Paul, for certain lines of railway running from the boundary, and that the charter had been refused by Mr. Roblin's government. I said that it had been asked for again last session and had been granted. The hon. gentleman denied this. I have here the statutes of Manitoba last year, chapter 59, page 56, and find in them a charter entitled ' An Act respecting the Midland Railway Company of Manitoba.' The lines of railway are thus defined :
Commencing at the city of Winnipeg and running in a southerly direction to a point on the international boundary at or near Emerson; also a line of railway to a point at or near Selkirk, also a line of railway to Brandon and Souris and the western boundary of the province, also a branch from Brandon to Minto and Boissevain, also a line of railway from Emerson to the village of Carman and thence to Portage la Prairie and thence to Winnipegosis, also a line from Emerson, Crystal City and Lauder and thence to the western boundary-I need not read the whole description. There are five points at which this railway touches the boundary line. The incorporators are Chas. S. Mellen, Henry P. Uplinm, Chas. G. Hamilton, John S. Ewart and James Fisher. The Grand Trunk Railway had nothing to do with that charter, and if the Minister of the Interior has such immense influence with the Premier of Manitoba, we had better keep him in power and raise his salary. Not only did the Manitoba government give these gentlemen a charter, but it is well understood that if they construct these lines, some 1.100 miles in extent, they will be assisted by the province.
Oh, no.

To the tune of $10,000 per mile. The whole questiou was thrashed out in the legislature, and it was generally agreed that if this company went on to construct those lines, it would get tlie same guarantee to its bonds as was given the Northern road.
Is that in the Journals of the House?

I wish just to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) the other night. I did not care then to take it up, because be made so many ridiculous statements that it was almost impossible to meet them all. He said that by the reduction of 2 cents per one hundred pounds on wheat last year the farmers saved $400,000, and that the saving this year would be $1,600,000 on the carriage of wheat to Port Arthur. But when you consider that only some 8,000,000 bushels of wheat was tributary in any possible shape to the Canadian Northern Railway, and that a great portion of it went to Duluth on which there was no reduction whatever, you will see that the largest amount that the farmers could possibly save would be $40,000 instead of $400,000, and this year it will be $80,000 instead of $1,600,000. But that is only a sample of the exaggerated statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria.) The charter that I referred to was asked for the session previous, and was then refused. The charter asked this year, and which was granted, was given to the Northern Pacific Railway, of which Mr. Mellen is president, and Mr. Armstrong solicitor. It is openly a Northern Pacific Railway charter. The hon. gentleman said that it got a guarantee of $3,500,000. He has the Journals of the House in front of him, and I challenge him to show that any guarantee was given. I say that it has not one cent of guarantee, and it never will.
Yes, it will.

While the hon. gentleman's head is frequently wrong, I know that his heart is right, and I am sure that he will rise and apologize for the misstatement he made. The thing stands exactly as I have said. The company that applied the previous year for a charter is not the company that applied this year. The company that was refused the year before is the organization which is at the back of this scheme to-day-a lot of Liberal politicians. With reference to the saving to the farmers by the reduction of freight rates, that saving was not effected on the wheat alone, but on all the products that went out and the goods brought in, and the estimate I gave is that given by the traffic managers of the various railways. And I may add. that when the great reduction which the Canadian Pacific Railway is making this year, owing to the policy of

the Roblin government in compelling the Canadian Northern to cut down its rates, comes into effect, it will be found that a saving of $1,500,000 will be well within the mark.
The hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) made the statement that the probability was that the Grand Trunk would go by way of Chicago. He admitted frankly, like a man, as he sometimes does in his better moments, that the Grand Trunk Railway had their line into Minneapolis to-day. The hon. gentleman found fault with me for objecting to that. Why, Sir, from the very start I have endorsed the Grand Trunk in their plan of going through Chicago, and I endorse them to-day. The only thing I ask is that they shall come out openly here, and tell us plainly what they are going to do, and not try to bunco the people of Canada by taking up this north shore line as a part of a great transcontinental system when they never intend to operate it or have anything to do with it. The hon. gentleman said that the Rlbe-ral-Conservative party entered into the arrangement to build the Canadian Pacific Railway without sufficient knowledge. Why, he knows that in the library and in the Department of Railways and Canals there are reports, which were laid on the Table of the House-and I am sure he has pored over them many a day-before the Canadian Pacific Railway was ever touched west of the city of Winnipeg, reports of surveyors who had been through every pass from the American boundary clean up to Peace river pass. The hon. gentleman knows that, or if he does not, he ought to know it, for those reports have been on file in the Department of Railways and Canals for thirty years. The hon. gentleman talks about an instrumental survey. No instrumental survey has ever been made from the Montreal river to the border of Manitoba passing north of Lake Nepigon. What is the object of the attempt made here fo deceive the House and the people by statements that tliei-e is evidence in regard to these things, when there is not ? If the hon. gentleman would frankly admit that the policy is to have a transcontinental road through by Chicago and on to the Pacific, their no fault will be found. It would be a mag nificent line and it would do Canada good Why ? They are running to Duluth. The hon. gentleman practically admitted that And we might as well admit it. Let us' face the facts squarely as they are. They will bring grain from Canadian and United States farming centres to Duluth, and they will tranship it by boat, as everybody knows, to Midland. That is the Grand Trunk part of it-other parts of the traffic will go to other Canadian ports. And, when the Georgian bay canal is completed, as I hope it will be
Hear, hear.

Yes, I have al
ways advocated that this should be done, though I happen to be more or less interested in seeing another part of our canal system developed. But I am not sectional, and I do not think any member of this House should be sectional in discussing these broad issues. When the Georgian bay canal is opened, trade will go that way. It need not be opened to a depth of 21 feet, for the carrying capacity of a canal depends not so much on its depth as on the length of its locks. We can have long barges of shallow draft with a capacity of 250,000 bushels, just as you can have shorter barges of deeper draft. With that canal completed through to Montreal, then, as was pointed out at this Minneapolis banquet by Mr. J. J. Hill, as I have read this afternoou, the trade not only of the great Canadian North-west, but of western and south-western United States, will find its outlet by Canadian ports. Run the line to Duluth ! It is going there, and the hon. gentleman knows it. He talks about it being provided that there should be a line to Nepigon. I cannot find it. I would ask the Minister of Justice, who seems to know something about it
I am informed that an amendment has been made in the Senate to provide for another Canadian port on Lake Superior. I understand this means Nepigon.

I suppose that the local member out there, Mr. Conmee, who has a charter which carries certain pulp wood and fishing concessions is getting his oar in and is working his little scheme-after having got these concessions from the province of Ontario-to get a rake-off from the Dominion treasury too.
He has come down here fishing.
Yes, and successfully. Let these gentlemen come out and say frankly and manfully that they are going to have this Duluth line. If they do, we will deal with them on the merits of the question.

The clause now under discussion by the committee is as follows :
Section 2,
The said agreement bearing date the 29th day of July. 1903, and a copy of which forms the schedule to this Act, is hereby ratified and confirmed and declared to be legally binding upon His Majesty and the said Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and His said Majesvy and the said company are hereby authorized and empowered to do whatever is necessary in order to give full effect to the said agreement.
It is all very well putting these things in an Act of parliament. But we have had experience in the past with regard to these tilings. I specially wish to direct the attention of the Committee and of the country to an agreement or under-

gave a certain concession to the public. I stand liere to-day and, on behalf of the people of Canada, demand that before a single dollar is given to the Grand Trunk or any company connected with it, it shall fulfil the obligation embodied in the Act of parliament which I have quoted, passed more than fifty years ago. It Is on questions like this that the people will judge this proposition when they come to deal with it. I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the government to this matter and of reminding them that they themselves have laid down the principle that, when assistance Is given to a company, concessions shall be demanded of that company in the interest of the people. At the very least, we should insist that the obligations to the public undertaken by the company shall be carried out. Now it is up to the government to-day to show their good faith and to show their intention of carrying out their obligation, to show that they intend to insist on the Grand Trunk fulfilling that obligation made more than fifty years ago.
It is outlawed.

I do not think it is. I do not think you can outlaw a good Act of parliament. But if the government do not insist on that, what guarantee have we that this agreement is worth the paper that it is written on ? Is this to be outlawed too ? Now, I call the attention of the Prime Minister to it, and also to the Canadian Pacific Railway agreement, where there is a solemn undertaking that the rates are to be regulated. I say that parliament is bound to see that these previous agreements are fulfilled before we give either of these companies a single dollar in addition. One is here to-day, the other will be here tomorrow, and they should not get a single dollar until these undertakings of former years have been carried out.

The hon. gentleman has referred to the Canadian Pacific Railway rates. Will he say where and when the Canadian Pacific Railway have exceeded the limit of the rate that was fixed for them in the Crow's Nest Pass road ?

Provision was made here for a reduction of the tolls on the Canadian Pacific Railway as soon as its earnings reached a certain percentage on the cost of construction. That is a matter to be ascertained, and should have been ascertained long ago, and the attention of the government has been called to it.

I did call the attention of the government to that the first session I was in the House, and I was then informed by one of the ministers that the company was not charging up to the limit of the rates it was entitled to, as fixed in that Act.
But I am pointing out that they never ascertained what the roadj cost.
It is being done now.
Now we are getting some information. Then what has been done in connection with the Grand Trunk Railway, and its non-fulfilment of its obligation ?
By way of information, would my hon. friend be good enough to say whether the penny-a-mile clause still exists in the Grand Trunk charter ?
It was in the charter under which they got this $50,000,000 public money.
I would like to know if that'section is still in the Grand Trunk charter, and if not, when it was repealed ?
I do not say it was repealed. If it was, it was after they got the people's money.
Let us be accurate. Does my hon. friend say it was not repealed ?

No, I do not say that,
I will not vouch for that. I will only say that there was an agreement between the Grand Trunk Railway Company of that day and the then government of Canada when they got a charter. They got the charter, and with it a promise of large financial assistance. They got the financial assistance. and as a condition the people of Canada received a promise of a parliamentary rate of two cents a mile. Now where is the performance of this undertaking ? There was an undertaking that they would give the public a two-cents-a-mile-rate. We have undertakings in this contract that the public will get certain things, and how are they to get them ? Will these undertakings be carried out ? I say the first thing the government should do in connection with this new agreement is to say to them : Before we sign this you must show your good faith by carrying out your former obligation to give the people a two-cent-a-mile-rate.

I want to ask the hon. member for North Norfolk a question. I see by the ' Globe ' of June 4th. referred to by another hon. member, that the hon. member for North Norfolk stated that Quebec would be kept open for navigation all winter. Now, I am certain that the hon. member never made a statement before the Railway Committee to influence his brother members there unless he had evidence sufficient to justify him in making such statement. I am perfectly satisfied therefore that when he made his statement he had evidence which at that time satisfied him that Que-328

bee harbour would be open all winter. Now,
I wound not for a moment suggest that the Minister of Justice had since persuaded him that that is not the fact, I am sure the Minister of Justice would be only too glad if it were the fact.
It is the fact.

I am very glad to hear the Minister of Justice corroborate the statement made by the hon. member for North Norfolk. Then if it is the fact that Quebec harbour is open all winter-I suppose nobody will dispute that it is open all summer-then why should not Quebec be our national port, and why extend the railway away beyond Quebec when we have there a harbour open the whole year round ? Therefore, since that has been stated by the hon. member for North Norfolk and corroborated on the floor of this House by the Minister of Justice, I now appeal to the Minister of Justice, as representative of the city of Quebec, to do justice to his constituents, and since he honestly believes- for we must suppose he would not otherwise have made the statement-that Quebec is a port open the whole year round, I ask him to do justice to his own port and to see that instead of attempting to carry grain uselessly away beyond Quebec to Moncton, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway should ship that grain the whole year'round from Quebec.

It is always well to be accurate. The hon. gentleman says it has been stated that the port of Quebec is open the whole year round. My recollection of the port of Quebec, covering now about fifty years, is that it has been closed in the winter, about a dozen times ; outside that the port of Quebec is open all winter. But I have never known any shipment of grain to be made from Quebec in the winter. As to my .constituents, I am responsible to them for my statements, and when the time comes my hon. friend will see what my constituents think of me.
Will my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Nortlirup) kindly send me the passage that he quoted from ?

As the hon. member for North Norfolk has asked to see this quotation, perhaps when he is answering me, he will be kind enough to give us further information, because it might be instructive, and enable us to come to a conclusion on certain other matters. I find that the member for North Norfolk recently made an address in his constituency recommending the present scheme, and in that address, which is reported in the ' Globe ' of the 25th of August, he so succeeded in working up the feelings of his audience that a motion was moved by a Mr. Wells, K.C., endorsing the scheme, and congratulating the

lion, gentleman on the eloquence with which he had presented it. Now, perhaps the lion, gentleman, while explaining his references to the port of Quebec, would be good enough to let us know whether this Mr. Wells who, on the 25th of August last, was a humble lawyer and has since been appointed to the bench of the province of Ontario- perhaps he will let us know whether his apointment to the bench was a reward for services rendered on the 25th of August, and whether it was that no other man could be got to move such a motion unless this inducement was held before him.

I will take the last point first. I may say with regard to the resolution moved by the joint associations of North and South Norfolk endorsing the railway policy of the government and presenting a flattering opinion as to my own services, that I was very much gratified at that expression of opinion. With regard to the statement quoted by my hon. friend
Who is Mr. Wells ?

Mr. Wells is a citizen of Canada, an elector of the county of Norfolk, and is entitled to make a motion if he chooses to do so, a privilege of which he availed himself on that occasion. With regard to the quotation made by my hon. friend, it seems great importance is attached to any statement that I make, especially if there is the remotest possibility of finding any tinge of inconsistency in me. The report in the ' Globe ' is necessarily an epitome of what was said.
He favoured Mr. Cochrane's suggestion and thought that Quebec could be kept open for navigation all winter.
Now, I remember very well the statement that was made upon that occasion, and in dealing with the question of keeping Quebec harbour open I expressed the opinion that it could "be done, and reiterate the expression of that opinion to-day. I pointed out [DOT]on that occasion the fact that the Baltic sea, which was formerly closed to navigation for several months of the year by ice, is now kept open by means of ice breakers, and that Kroonstadt can be reached at any time by the operation of these huge ice breakers, which can make their way with ease through ice ten feet thick, and that I saw no reason why, if the Baltic sea is kept open, Quebec, which is naturally open most of the time, could not be made available to navigation in winter.

My hon. friend beside me has made a prophecy; I hope it will be realized. He tells us that there is no doubt whatever that within a short time tiie railways will be able to carry grain more cheaply than it can be carried by water route. He is going to prove that to us.
Three cents a bushel less.

Yes, if he can do so he will be a great man-he is already a great man I can see-but he will be a greater man. My hon. friend, I very much fear, is not as accurate as he has been in the past when he has carefully studied a question.
I- suppose my hon. friend would not wish to put me in a false position.
Certainly not.
I referred to the water and rail route.
Certainly, I take issue just on that point. My hon. friend puts up the all-rail against the all-water route, is not that it ?	[DOT]
No, I put up the allrail route against transportation from the west by rail and water.

Very well, my hon. friend says he put up the all-rail route against the route by rail and water. I take issue with him on that basis. My hon. friend knows this continent as well as any other man, he knows very well, for instance, that between Chicago and New York, by rail, the distance is 912 miles; between Chicago and Buffalo there are 412 miles by rail and 900 miles by water. In spite of that it cannot be controverted that the water route is constantly gaining on the rail route. So much is this the case, that the rates on the water-ways are now so much Tower than by rail during last year on Lake Superior alone it has been established by official statistics, $63,000,000 have been saved, that is, taking the rates as they have been paid on the water-ways and ns they are charged on the rail route, $63,000,000 have been saved.

A year ?
Hon. Ml-. TARTE. Last year only, and on Lake Superior only. I quoted the other day from an address delivered by Mr. Noble, president of the American Society of Engineers, who gave these figures in June last.
My hon. friend knows there will be 1,500 miles between Winnipeg and Quebec by the new road andt perhaps there will be 100 miles more. There are 1,500 miles between Winnipeg and Quebec. How, in heaven's name, can he expect to compete against grain, for instance, from Chicago to New York, a distance of 900 miles, against the line between Chicago and Philadelphia. 820 miles; against Chicago to Baltimore, 812 miles-how can my hon. friend hope to compete? It is out of the question. My hon. friend will let me tell him that he is simply serving unwittingly the cause of American ports, nothing short of it. I charge him with helping unwittingly the American ports against Canadian ports, and the reason is

obvious, the charge is proved by the fact itself. The American water-ways charge 1} cents a bushel from Duluth or Chicago to the port of Buffalo. The American railways charge 3 cents from Buffalo to New York. How can my hon. friend expect to be able to compete by Ills all-rail scheme against freights like these ? My hon. friend knows right well that our American friends are to-day contemplating the deepening and widening of the Erie Canal. The present rate on a bushel of grain on the Erie Canal is on an average 24 cents. They expect to reduce that by one-half cent, which would make a rate from Chicago to New York of 2 or 24 cents. They are contemplating also deepening the Detroit and Ste. Marie rivers from 19 to 20 feet, which would increase the capacity of their boats 10 per cent and decrease the rates proportionately. The only policy by which we can compete with our American friends in carrying out, not only our own freight but their freight, is by the development of our water-ways. That is the only way to do it, and any other exclusively railway policy we may adopt will be simply playing into the hands of American people and American ports. My hon. friend (Mr. Charlton) should not do that. He is a well-posted man, one of the best posted in the House, and he knows that the figures I give are correct. He lias himself given them in the House. I rise to protest with all the energy I can put in my words against the policy he has suggested. Let the friends of the government andi some of us who have independent views
No.

adian trade from the west to east, but American trade as well. Let us improve our harbours and let us develop our rail connection with the Georgian bay, and then we will be able to compete with the Americans, but otherwise we cannot. My hon. friend from North Norfolk knows that the means he suggests is not the proper means to develop the trade within this country from a transcontinental standpoint. He will have to prove first that the history of American transportation is a lie, and if he can prove that we will be glad to listen to him. I take exception to a statement made by a gentleman on the other side; that during the last few years we have been doing nothing to relieve the congestion in the west. Well, Sir, we have started in the right direction. We have started to improve the St. Lawrence route from the Straits of Belle Isle to Montreal, and we have started to improve our ports on the lakes. When I was Minister of Public Works, I preached the gospel of transportation as much as 1 could, but I often found myself in the presence of deaf ears, and I was met with the answer that I was asking too much money from parliament It is my determined opinion that we have proceeded too slowly. We should have equipped our water-ways and harbours twenty-five years ago, and because we did not do so, is the reason why we have not diverted the trade from American centres. One of the reasons why the North-west has not developed as rapidly as it should have, is because we have not given to our waterways the attention that they deserve, and if we did give them attention, they would have cheapened the means of transportation to the farmers of the west. I am glad for one that the Grand Trunk is going into the west. We have listened to many patriotic speeches, in which we are told that the present policy of the government is to build a railway on Canadian soil all through. But the fact that we will build a railway on Canadian soil from Port Simpson to Moncton does not prove that we will handle the trade. Facts are stronger than words, words do not always mean much in this world. Now, what is the Grand Trunk going to do ? Having the map in our hands are we sure that at some future date the Grand Trunk will not make an arrangement with the Northern Pacific, or the Great Northern to handle their trade through Duluth or through Chicago. What guarantee is given to us in this contract on that very important point ? The Grand Trunk is partly an American railway and partly a Canadian railway and that is no crime. They ha ve been carrying freight to Portland 330 miles further than Montreal for the same rate tbat they are charging to Montreal. That is a fact which cannot be disputed by any business man. They have been obliged to do it because they have invested $25.000.000 in their Portland line. I grant you that we have not sufficient accommodation Hon. Mr. TARTE.
in Montreal. Now let us remember that the Grand Trunk to-day is located in Minneapolis and St. Paul, and from Duluth to these cities it is only, I think, 150 miles. If we do not take means to keeji tbat trade within our boundaries it may get away from us, and we may wake up some fine morning to find that we have had a very bad dream. These are facts that should be discussed not from a party standpoint, but from a business standpoint. I do not wish to lecture the House, but I do say that this is a business matter and not a party matter. We will be judged by what we are doing at the present time. The geographical position should not be ignored. What means will the government take to prevent an arrangement by which the trade of the North-west will be diverted to those American points ? I am asking the question because I think we should now make the future safe. If we do not improve our own water-ways, where is the trade going to go ? During the last four or five years, I have heard our excellent friends from the west over and over again telling us that they do not care for the St. Lawrence route, but they want to ship their grain as cheaply as they can, and they have spoken to us of Duluth and other American points. We are face to face with a great responsibility. We have been told that we did not take any precautions of this kind when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was incorporated ; but the position then was not the same as it is now. The Canadian Pacific Railway was to be a Canadian railway; it was not located partly in the United States and partly in Canada. It seems to me that these matters deserve the consideration of the right hon. leader of the government and his friends.

I am not going to make a speech. I only want to say that I do not agree with the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte). I have had experience in the transportation business ; I operated canal boats between Montreal and New York, and schooners through Lake Champlain ; and I want to say that I was driven out of business by railway competition. The Delaware and Hudson River Railway was built along Lake Champlain from New York to Montreal, and it killed the transportation business by boats.
How long ago was that ?

About thirty years ago. Before the railway was built the business was very good ; but the railway drove me out of business, and I knew enough to sell my boats and quit. I could not compete against the railway, and we all know that in the United States the canals are being closed up by railway competition. There are six or seven canals in the United States already closed by railway competition.
How deep are those canals ?

I can tell the hon. gentleman one of the canals that was closed, and he can measure it if he likes. The great canal from Philadelphia to Pittsburg, 300 miles long, was closed by railway competition. They built a railway alongside of that canal, with 100-ton engines and 100-pound rails, and they closed up the canal. Two hundred miles of it have been closed for the last ten years. There are several other canals in the United States that have been closed by railway competition, and I think it is a useless expenditure of money digging canals, inland canals at any rate. There might be something in opening up natural water-ways ; but when you take into consideration the fact that a canal is closed for six months in the year, that your capital is idle all that time, and that the canal has to pay during the summer or you cannot operate it, I think it is a waste of money digging canals. The improvement in railways has settled the transportation question. 1 believe the railways will carry wheat from Winnipeg to Quebec cheaper than it can be carried by the water-ways, because they can haul it the year round. I have no doubt of that in my own mind, and that is the reason I supported this scheme. I am opposed to digging any more canals. We have spent perhaps $80,000,000 on canals in Canada, which do not pay a cent of revenue, and the people of this country are getting tired mf spending their money and not getting any return for it. This railway is going to pay ; I have no doubt about that. It is going to open up millions of acres of land. When hon. gentlemen get up in this House and say that a railway with a 21-foot grade cannot be built through that country, I do not think they know what they are talking about. You can build a railway anywhere with a 21-foot grade if you have a mind to spend the money to do it. You are not obliged to go over mountains ; you can go under them. My opinion is that the Grand Trunk people would never have undertaken this scheme if they were not satisfied that they could build a railway and make it pay. There is no common sense in the argument which I have heard in this House that these people are going to undertake a scheme which they cannot carry through. They are not shysters, and to my mind there is not a word of truth in that statement. In the United States they are not enlarging their canals. The hon. member for St. Mary's says that they are talking about enlarging the Erie canal. They have been talking about that for the last ten years ; but they are a sensible people, and they will not fool away their money in that way. Only about one-tenth of the grain carried from Buffalo to New York goes by the Erie canal ; and I was told that the railway people offered to carry the grain free if they were paid the interest on what the enlargement of the canal would cost. In my
opinion, canals are out of date. They might do for the old days, but they will not do for the present day. This government, Mr. Speaker, has brought this country out of the dark days of 1896 to the prosperous days of 1903 ; and I want to say right here that the Liberals are the people, and our leader is the greatest statesman in Canada. The present government have increased the revenue of this country from $38,000,000 up to $66,000,000, and they have the money to build this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or any other railway that they choose to build. A tariff for revenue is the true policy for this country-not a tariff for manufacturers, but a tariff for the whole people of Canada. The whole people of Canada get the benefit of the revenue tariff, and not the manufacturers alone. What did hon. gentlemen opposite tell us ? They told us that manufacturers were going to employ enough help to eat up all the products of the Northwest, and create a home market for all the grain of the North-west and all our butter and cheese. But that is all humbug. The opposition to-day are trying to get back into power. They started a show some twenty-five years ago, and they had on their bill boards ' Protection,' and they humbugged the country for eighteen years. But in 1896 the bubble burst, the present government came into power, and the country is prosperous. They may obstruct this House all they like, but when they have to face the electorate at the next election, their numbers will be diminished less than ever.

I would not ask the indulgence of the House, but for the fact that the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has made some allusions to myself, and rather cast an aspersion upon my political honesty.
