He made the assertion that a transcontinental railway cannot compete with a part rail and part water route from the North-west to the sea. I maintain that it can, and my hon. friend asserts that in this I am misleading the public. I wish to deal svith that one particular point, and I start out by the assertion that the grain from the Northwest can be carried by the proposed transcontinental line, when completed, to the seaboard more cheaply than by rail and water -by rail to Port Arthur and by water either to Parry Sound or to Buffalo, and by rail thence to New York or Montreal. The average freight rates from Chicago to New York for the year 1902 by all-rail were 9-94 for corn, and 10:62 for wheat. By lake and canal they were 4-83 for corn and 5-57 for wheat. By lake and rail they were for corn 5-51, and for wheat 5 89. ' Chicago is a point that corresponds with Duluth or Port Arthur, and we may take these rates as applicable to those points. Or a rate of 5-89. practically six cents per 'bushel from Port Arthur to New York by water and

rail or about the same from Port Arthur to Montreal. We have to add the cost of transportation from the prairies to Port Arthur. The rate from Brandon to Port Arthur has recently been reduced. It is now fourteen cents per hundred pounds, or 8'40 per bushel. Adding 8-40 to six makes 14-40, or practically fourteen and a half cents per bushel from Brandon to New York or Montreal- by rail to Port Arthur, by vessel to Buffalo or Parry Sound, and by rail from Buffalo or Parry Sound to New York or Montreal. Can that grain be transported from Brandon to Quebec for that figure, fourteen and a half cents per bushel or less ? If it can be transported for fourteen and a half cents, then the rates by rail and water are practically the same from Brandon to the seaboard as they are by all-rail.
If I am well informed, this year the rates on the Canadian Northern Railway from Brandon to Port Arthur are between five and six cents.

Ffom Winnipeg to Port Arthur on the Canadian Northern Railway up to yesterday the rate was twelve cents per hundred pounds. It will be ten cents from this out. The Order in Council was passed on the ltltli of July. It was fourteen cents over the Canadian Pacific Railway.

From Duluth to Quebec it cost only three cents per bushel and even less this year. But even if it costs seven cents, the rate will certainly decrease between western points and the outlet, it will certainly come down to three or four cents per bushel. Then you will be face to face with a rate of about six cents by rail and water to Quebec.
That is in addition to the rate to Port Arthur.

To-day the Wolvin boats are taking to the port of Quebec wheat at three cents per bushel. They have taken it occasionally at two and a half cents, but the average rate this summer is three cents. The rates are the same from Port Arthur and Fort William. Now the Canadian Northern Railway has charged this year seven cents.
Six cents.

That makes nine cents from the wheat fields to Quebec. The rate from Port Arthur, Duluth and other western points will certainly come down. But take them as they are now, and the railways are out of court.

That remains to be seen. I would ask permission to complete my statement without interruption. The rate from Brandon to Port Arthur was sixteen cents per hundred pounds up to yesterday. Yesterday it was reduced to fourteen cents or 8 40 a bushel. If my hon.
friend is correct about the rate from Port Arthur to Quebec, that makes 1140 or eleven and a half cents.
Hear, hear.
There never has been a bushel of wheat carried by water from Port Arthur to Quebec.

I am proceeding on the assumption that the hon. member foist. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is correct. I know what the rate is to-day from Brandon to Port Arthur, and I know that it has been reduced, but I have no right to presume that it will be reduced further. I take his statement that the rate from Port Arthur to Quebec is three cents, but 1 cannot suppose that that will be the normal rate. I do not believe it, as a matter of fact, but, for the purpose of this argument I accept his statement that the rate from Port Arthur to Quebec is three cents per bushel. I assert that the present rate is 8 40 cents per bushel from Brandon to Port Arthur. What can it be carried for by rail?
Would the hon. gentleman tell us what the distance is ?

I just wish to get through this statement. I have been interrupted to-day at every second or third sentence. I have data with regard to the cost of transportation furnished me by Mr. .1. G. Scott, of the Great Northern Railway. That gentleman states that there is one division of that road where the grades are 6-10ths or 31 68-IOOth feet to the mile. With a Mogul engine weighing seventy-five tons without the tender, they draw on that division loads of 2.000 or 2,020 tons. That is equivalent to forty-five cars loaded with 1.000 bushels of wheat each, or 45.000 bushels of wheat to the train. And the cost of performing that work on this road was eighty-nine cents per train mile-that is for every mile travelled by the train. Let us place that at one dollar, instead of eighty-nine cents. And let us suppose that we have a road from Brandon to Quebec having similar grades. The distance is given us at 1,475 miles from Quebec to Winnipeg. That is in excess of what it actually is, but let us take those figures. The cost of hauling over that road on the basis of the figures I have given would be 3 58 cents per bushel. Add to this fifty per cent profit and you have 5 37 cents per bushel as the cost of transporting grain from Brandon to Quebec, with a profit of fifty per cent. I put this against my hon. friend's statement that it can be sent by part rail and part water at 11-40 cents. The hon. gentleman says that the all-rail is not in it. Why, Sir, the water route Is not in it. Now that we are in a position to make calculations, we find surprising results. Let us see what this traffic can be done for on a 4-10 grade. On such a grade, an engine of the character I have stated can haul sixty ears loaded with 1,000

bushels to the ear, or 60,000 bushels, | amounting to 1,800 tons. That is a model

ate load for these engines on a line with these grades, with heavy rails, massive bridges and the other modern equipment required. They could handle seventy cars just as well, but that the train would be unwieldy. 1 live on a road where they can haul one hundred cars with a grade of nineteen feet. With a 4T0 grade from Brandon to Quebec the actual cost of hauling would be 2-68 cents per bushel. Add 134 cent-that is, add fifty per cent for profit-and you will find that grain can be hauled at 4 02 cents from Brandon to Quebec with a road such as I have described and still allow a profit of fifty per cent. Some lion, gentlemen tell us that this road cannot solve the transportation problem, but that it will be a failure. My hon. friend tells us that the government scheme cannot be justified on transportation grounds. I say that the most magnificent and conclusive of all the demonstrations thut can be afforded ns to the wisdom of the government's project will be its results on transportation grounds. I do not wish to go further into the question, but I thought these remarks should be made in answer to my hon. friend.

The figures that have been quoted, let me say with all deference to Mr. Scott, are fancy figures. In this discussion we have before us the results of the experience of the greatest railways in the world. There are 200,000 miles of railways in the United States, managed by able men, running through a thickly settled country with a population of 80,000,000. There is not one single railway among them that charges such rates as the hon. gentleman quotes. These are simply figures on paper, figures which cannot be upheld by experience. There is nothing easier than to dream of figures, to play with figures. But what is the experience ? Where are the facts which my hon. friend (Mr. Charlton), well-posted as he is, can give us to show that these figures have any sense in them ? That is the word I mean-any sense in them. If the hon. gentleman can give me the case of any railway on the other side of the line whose rates are within one hundred per cent of the figures lie has quoted, I shall have no more to say. These rates are fancy rates, rates made by a man of good will, a very enthusiastic man. We have heard him before the Railway Committee. I had these figures in my own hands. Mr. Scott sent them to me. I was carried away with them at first. But I have discussed them with able men, men well-informed in railway business, and I have been shown that there is no reason in them. They cannot be established by the statistics and by experience.

The hon. gentleman asks what are the facts. I quoted the facts.
1 gave Mr. Scott as authority for the fact
that on a certain portion of their track, with certain power, they had hauled 2,000 to 2.020 tons, equivalent to 45,000 bushels of wheat, at a cost of eighty-nine cents per train mile. But I called it one dollar per train mile, adding eleven cents, to be sure J to cover the cost. These are data on which to base an absolute calculation. If the data are correct, the calculation proves itself. The hon. gentleman asks, where are the American roads that charge these rates ? Last year, in discussing this question of transportation, I showed on the authority of a New York Central official that the New York Central could, if necessary, at fifty cents per ton from Buffalo to New York, or at the rate of l-6 cent per bushel, and still yield profit enough to make it an object to do the business. We have made wonderful improvements in railway transportation in recent years. With level roads, heavy rails, massive bridges, the fish-plate joint, making a practically continuous rail, powerful locomotives which will carry five times the load of locomotives of a few years ago, with cars of large carrying capacity, with longer trains managed with the same force of crew, we see that the future is with rail transportation. We see that this transcontinental road will do the business of the country and will lay down the traffic at Canadian ports.

What are the New York Central rates ? In the winter months, five cents per bushel, from Buffalo to New 'York, a distance of only 440 miles. My hon. friend knows that well. And, in the summer months their rates are three and a half cents per bushel. I do not see how the hon. gentleman can quote the case of the New Y'ork Central. He gives us the opinion of a man who tells us. that he can do so and so. I believe Mr. Scott has not carried grain in quantities.
He has not carried it at all.
Then, his figures are not based upon experience, and should not be accepted.
What dividend is the New York Central paying ?
I shall not go into that question now.
On watered stock, $500 of which represents only $100 cash investment, they pay 5 to 6 per cent.
But they are not carrying grain only.

This questiou of the cost of carrying grain from the North-west to the sea-board is probably the most important one in connection with this transcontinental project. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said a little while ago that hon. gentlemen on this side had quoted his assertions very frequently

in respect to this matter, and more often than any one else. The reason for that is that the hon. gentleman has made more definite statements in respect to this matter than the members of the government have, and there has been in some of his statements something to go on, and something to criticise, whereas the members of the government have been very general in their statements regarding the cost of transportation. Now, I do not want to misquote the hon. member for North Norfolk, but I understood him to say a few moments ago that the rate from the head of the lakes to Buffalo was six cents a bushel.
My hon. friend evidently does not take in statements readily. I said from the head of the lakes to New York or Montreal, six cents a bushel.
From the head of the lakes ?
From the head of the lakes to Montreal.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. He meant to say the rate from the head of the lakes to the sea-board was six cents a bushel.
Yes.

Now the hon. gentleman was endeavouring to compare the rate from the head of the lakes to the sea-board by existing routes, with a rate which he proposed to figure out over this new line, and he used six cents a bushel in this case.
I used, in addition to that, the cost from Brandon to the lake.

The hon. gentleman from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) accused the member for North Norfolk of not always being accurate in his assertions. Whether that is so or not, I would like to say to the member for St. Mary's that it is not necessary to bring proof to upset what the hon. gentleman has said here this afternoon with regard to freight rates, because we have his own words. He stated a few moments ago that the rate from the head of the lakes to the sea-board is six cents a bushel. But in May last, speaking on this transportation question, he said this :
That tradie will seek the waters of the great chain of lakes.
He went on to say :
So you have the possibility of carrying wheat from Port Arthur to New York for three cents a bushel.
Not six cents a bushel, as he states now.

Will my hon. friend allow me to explain ? I was speaking then of possibilities, and not of conditions existing. I said in that speech that wheat had been carried from the upper lakes to Buffalo for a cent and a half a bushel, and that it could be carried from Buffalo to New York for one cent and six mills. But I did not say it was being done, and I do
not believe it will be. But even if it were done, with that rate from Brandon to Port Arthur we can beat them-even at three cents a bushel.

The hon. gentleman says he was speaking with regard to possibilities and that he didn't suppose these possibilities would ever be realized. Then X suppose that we are to take in the same way the statements he made this afternoon with regard to carrying freight from Brandon over this Grand Trunk Pacific to Quebec, I suppose we are to treat them as possibilities which will not be realized.

My hon. friend should be fair enough to give me credit for telling this House that the;! work can be performed from Brandon to Quebec for a certain figure. If a fair profit is added to the actual naked cost, it will make a certain figure. Now let him controvert that statement if he can. But to say that I said something in May last, perhaps upon insufficient data, that conflicts with something I say to-day, has nothing to do with the argument unless he chooses to assume that I am an ass who never changes his opinion.

I will read the rest:
So you have the possibility of carrying wheat from Port Arthur to New York for 'three cents a bushel, or at most four cents a bushel. Now these are conditions which render it, in my opinion, impossible at present to compete with that route. It is useless to think of hauling wheat from a point as far west as Port Arthur by an all-rail route to Quebec, or to Halifax, at prices ouch as those I quoted with regard to the American lines.
So if the hon. gentleman blames us for quoting him too frequently, he must remember that he is inconsistent in his statements. Now, Mr. Chairman, I contend that it is an absurd proposition for the hon. gentleman to say that wheat can be carried from Brandon to Quebec for four cents a bushel. I do not understand how the hon. gentleman arrives at his figures. All railway statistics point to a certain cost of doing business, under certain conditions. If you have favourable gradients and favourable curves in your railway, you can do business for a certain rate per ton per mile. If these gradients are unfavourable it costs more. Now the lowest cost at which grain can be carried per ton per mile, or any other kind of freight, according to the statistics which have been furnished us, is from five mills per ton per mile to four mills per ton per mile, and under extremely favourable conditions, it can be carried for perhaps three or three and a half mills per ton per mile. The fact is that the rates which exist at present from the head of the lakes to the seaboard are half what it would cost if these figures were computed, and I challenge the hon gentleman to contradict me. It will cost double the rates that exist to

carry grain from Winnipeg to Quebec by rail, and you cannot possibly expect that road to be a grain carrying road. I think that the best thing the government can do in regard to this question is to get some expert testimony. Why can't they get a letter from some prominent railway man of unquestionable authority on this question backing up the statements which are made by the member for North Norfolk ? Why don't they have some evidence as to this matter before us ?
They cannot get any. Let them get a letter from Sir William Van Horne.

Yes, or from Mr. Hays. Let Mr. Hays, over his own signature, tell us that grain can be carried on this road for four cents a bushel. Grain is not. carried at any such price over the Grand Trunk system, nor for double that price.
But this discussion started out in regard to the question of the location of this road, and we have been wandering all over the field. I have been trying to get on my feet once or twice to ask some questions. In the Grand Trunk Pacific charter the principle is laid down that this road will be thirty miles at least away from existing roads excepting at the terminals, and we asked the government the question whether they were going to adhere to that principle or not. In the Railway Committee the exMinister of Railways and Canals, in the early part of this session, was candid with the committee, and he stated that the government were prepared to lay that down as a principle, not only with regard tc this road but in regard to other roads, and that no charters would be granted to railways in the North-west unless they were thirty miles away from any existing road. He thought at first it should be forty miles, but afterwards the distance was reduced to thirty. Now the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) this morning, when the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and the Prime Minister were discussing this matter, came into the discussion and illustrated the matter in this way : He said there are railroads running from here to Montreal, or as you go into Montreal, there are two railroads alongside of each other, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and there you have competition. Now, he says, you will have competition with this road which will run alongside of the Canadian Northern Railway. Well, that is a question. I do not think there is any competition in two railroads running alongside each other, because the rates are already fixed. But that is not what we want. We want to know whether the government intend to force the Canadian Northern Railway to sell out to the Grand Trunk Railway. If that is not the policy of the government, will they say that this railroad will be at least thirty
miles away from existing lines, and that the principle laid down in the charter is going to be adhered to ? Now, something has been said in regard to the location of the eastern section of this road, and I admit that may be a matter of some difficulty. But there is one point upon which I would like some information. Why is it that there is not something in the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific stating what the grades are to be on that road ? We are having assertions here all the time ot the fact that this railroad is going to carry the products of the North-west to the seaboard, and that it will carry them cheaply and economically.	.
If that is the case the road must oe well built because it must be a road with easy grades and easy curves. Yet there is nothing said in the contract in regard to the standard of the eastern section. If the government build a road which has five-tenths per cent grades or grades more difficult than five-tenths per cent, will the Grand Trunk Railway consider that they are bound to operate that road ? It appears to me that they would be able to repudiate the agreement altogether unless something definite is said in the contract in regard to the standard of the road. This road certainly cannot carry grain to compete with a water-route from the head of the lake to the seaboard, but what hope would there be of carrying grain or any other kind of produce unless it is built in the very best way, unless the grades are of the easiest. The arrangements in this respect appear to lie very loose and I hope that we will get some more light in regard to that. I do not desire to take up the time of the House now, as I wish to refer to these matters again, but I will say that if grain can oe carried by this road as cheaply or more cheaply than by water, why do the government hesitate to say that grain will be carried over this road at a less rate than the rates now in force to the sea-board. The Manitoba government in their agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway and in the consolidation of the Northern Pacific Railway with the Manitoba system said : You must reduce your rate of freight two cents by such a date and two cents more by such a date. The farmers of the Northwest could understand that agreement and they know that any grain shipped over that road is worth that much more per bushel to them. Will the government venture to say that grain will be carried by this new road one-half or one-quarter or one cent or two cents cheaper than at present. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said the rate would be three cents less than the existing rates to the sea-board. If the government would put something like that in the Bill that would be something that the people would understand, let the amount be as small as you like even if it is only one-quarter of a cent a bushel.

There is one thing to which I would wish to draw attention. We are all anxious to do an increasing trade with the mother country and one feature with reference to that trade was brought to our attention at the recent congress of the Board of Trade of the Empire Congress in Montreal? It is a matter which I think we should take into careful consideration. Complaint was made and I believe truly made that the quality of the grain which they received in the old country was not up to the standard. That statement was made publicly on the floor of the congress by reliable men and it was not disputed by our own people who were there. One question asked was :	Is there any way by which
we can go to the farmers of the Northwest. buy their grain direct and land that identical grain at our mills in the old country without any fear of its having been contaminated i One way in which we can solve this problem is by building a railway from Quebec to Winnipeg. Then, they can go to the farmers there and buy No. 1 hard for what the English merchant at the congress said they were willing to give shillings a hundred more-these were the identical words of the gentleman who made the complaints, ' shillings a hundred more '-if they were going to get the identical grain which they purchased in the west. If these people could buy grain in the west, put it in a car. haul it direct to Quebec, put that identical grain which they purchased into a compartment in a vessel and take it to their own sea-port, then they would know that they were getting their own grain. This matter was talked over privately with some of these gentlemen and when it was explained that it could be done with regard to wheat they asked whether it could be done in the case of oats. They said :	We
want a superior quality of oats, we want your white oats of the best grade and heaviest quality to make meal in our own country. The gentleman who asked this was assured that it could be done in the same way and then he asked if it could be done with pease. He said they wanted pease grown on our clay soils for cooking purposes on the other side because they said that pease grown on the clay soil will boil and mash down when others will not. These are practical men and they said : If there is any way in which these difficulties can be removed we will be able to' pay more for these products; under present conditions grain during shipment from the west must necessarily be mixed as it is handled in so many different ways ; a man buys grain in the west and it is put into an elevator with wheat of all qualities even although it is graded No. 1 hard, it will not be No. 1 hard when it reaches Liverpool. The reply of the Chairman of the Board of Trade of Montreal was that the grain was not tested in Montreal, but in Winnipeg and Port Arthur and that they were not responsible for the grading. The grain goes into the Mr. KEMP.
elevator in Winnipeg or wherever it is purchased in the west. Then it is placed in cars and mixed with other grain. It is elevated at Port Arthur and again mixed. It is placed in a boat and mixed again. It goes to Parry Sound, is placed in an elevator and mixed again, then it is put 111 tIle cars and where further mixing takes place and from there it is hauled to Montreal, where it is put in the vessel and still further mixed with other grain. There is no possibility of getting to Liverpool the actual grain which was originally purchased in the west. However, with through road from Winnipeg to Quebec the cars would be loaded with the identical grain the man purchased and would be taken through to Quebec. where the grain would be put into compartments in vessels, then the purchasers would get the identical grain purchased, which is what they want ; if they can do that, they say they are prepared to give shillings a hundred more for the grain than they otherwise would.
Can they not do that by the Canadian Pacific Railway now ?

I give the gentleman's identical words, and gentlemen who were present at the meeting of congress will recall them. The words were that they were prepared to give shillings a hundred more. One can easily understand that they want to get the very highest grade of wheat and want to know when they are paying for that that they are really getting it. " Our friends opposite talk as if there was nothing but wheat to be brought from the west. They must understand that cattle are raised there in increasing numbers and that you cannot carry cattle in the same way as you can wheat. You cannot dump cattle into an elevator and into cars and boats and elevate them again as you can grain. We want this railway in order to carry cattle by it. We want it to carry the cheese which will be raised in increasing quantities in the west; we want it to carry the butter which will be raised in increasing quantities there and we want these products to go by a through route so that they will not be injured In their passage. This road will be a good thing for the country, and every man interested in the welfare of this country will do well to vote for and support it in every way he can.

I want to refer to the calculation that was made by the hon member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and I am sorry that he is not here for it seems to me that the calculation was so unfair that it should not be allowed to pass unnoticed. In his calculation in regard to the cost of drawing wheat from Brandon to Quebec a few minutes ago he said that it would be drawn by the new line at four cents a bushel. Then he went on to show that it is taken now from Brandon to Port Arthur for 8-41 cents or nearly 8} cents a

busliel. Now it is carried by rail there and if he had allowed the same proportion of reduction upon that part of the trip which was only by rail there would have been more fairness in it, but he takes the crude rate that is now charged by rail. But although the charge for 560 miles rail is now 81 cents he says we can draw it by rail for 1,900 miles over the new line for 4 cents a bushel. Does it not seem absurd to say that that comparison is a reasonable one V There is no sense in the world in the comparison, because if you can reduce the rate to that extent between Brandon and Quebec, you can reduce it as well proportionately between Brandon and Fort Arthur. It is only a three cent rate from Port Arthur to Quebec by water and if-you make the same proportionate reduction between Port Arthur and Brandon, that the hon. gentleman proposes to make on his all-rail carriage between Port Arthur and Quebec, you will still have the rate by the water-route very much cheaper than by rail. There is nothing in that comparison. If the hon. gentleman can improve the carrying power of his railway, and so reduce the rates, that same improvement will apply to the railways between Port Arthur and Brandon or between Parry Harbour and Montreal or Quebec. The existing lines are as susceptible of the same improvements as you are going to put on the new line. Grain is carried from Port Arthur to Parry Harbour for one cent a bushel or less. No matter what calculation the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) makes, he will find that the rail and water route is still the cheapest.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Wright) made a long argument to show that as one of the necessities for this railway, we would be able to take No. 1 hard at Winnipeg, and deliver the same No. 1 hard at the sea-board. Why can not that be done to-day ?

I gave an illustration of how the wheat was handled, and my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) knows it, because he is an old grain dealer as well as I am. He knows very well that the grain is taken into the elevator at say Portage La Prairie, and that when they take the wheat from the farmers they grade it. It all goes to the elevator, and afterwards it is taken into the cars and comes to Port William, and there it is mixed again in the elevator. Thence it goes into the steamboats, and all kinds are mixed together, and are graded perhaps as No. 1, but they are not all No. 1 by any means.
You are all wrong.
I have been in the business, and I know it, and those gentlemen in Montreal who spoke at the Congress of the Chambers of Commerce, complained that they did not get all No. 1 hard.
What is your government inspector doing ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not answered my question. How does your new line affect the matter at all ? You have your train of cars alongside the elevator and you fill these cars with No. 1 hard, and you send it over this new railway to the ocean port. Why, the same thing is being practically done every day.
The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do, that when the wheat is taken from the farmers by the dealers they do the grading to suit themselves.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What arrangement is the hon. gentleman going to substitute for that when he has his new transcontinental road? Is he going to gather it from the farmers along the track, and put it on the cars V Mr. WRIGHT. This gentleman at Montreal argued, that the farmers have sent him perfect samples of No. 1 hard, and he wanted to buy that wheat direct from the farmers, so that he would get it equal to sample.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You can do that to-day on the Canadian Pacific Railway. You can buy (he wheat direct from the flat warehouses, direct from the farmers and carry it through on the Canadian Pacific Railway cars. That has been done in my section of the country by farmers who wanted No. t hard for seed, if these English gentlemen want to do that they can do it, but it is impracticable from a commercial point of view, even if you had your new road.

As it is near six o'clock, I would call the attention of the Prime -Minister to the fact, that we sat up very late last night, and it has been suggested that possibly we could get along as quickly with the work if we adjourned at six o'clock.
I think it would not in any way lengthen the debate if we did that. At least that is the wish that has been expressed to me.
I may tell my right hon. friend that there is no desire at all to delay the committee. We wish to do our duty in regard to the discussion of this scheme, but there is no idea whatever of delaying unduly the progress of the Bill.	,

I would be very anxious to meet the convenience of my hon. friends on the other side, and all the more readily because we would share in the benefit of the suggestion. I must remark, however, that we have been all day on this Bill, and that we have not passed one clause. I believe that the discussion has been important, although some parts of it were more or less academic.
This is a most important clause.
I do not find fault at all with the nature of the discussion to-day, but I would like my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) to tell me that we will pass this Bill within a reasonable delay. I should be
glad to comply with his request, but it would be upon the understanding that we shall pass this measure within some reasonable time.

I can not take that responsibility, particularly in view of the fact that I am only here in the position of a vicegerent. I think, however, there is a disposition to proceed with the Bill in a business-like way, provided my hon. friend gives us the information we require in a business-like way. There is not the slightest desire to obstruct the passage of this Bill. That is as much as I can say, and I think it is the feeling of my colleagues.

As to the information my hon. friend has asked for, the government cannot give any more information than we have given already. We could go on debating for days, but it will not be possible to give any more information than we have given at the present time, because it is impossible to say where that line will be located until the surveys are made on the ground, and until we have reports and have made a selection from the reports made to us. So far as that goes,
I have given you all the information that I can give.

This clause that is now before the committee is the all important clause, and the fact is that it will be the only one to discuss in connection with the whole Bill. If this clause went by, the whole Bill might go by. I may say that there is a great deal of information wanted yet in connection with this measure, and there is a good deal of information that can be given from this side of the House.

I have no objection to every reasonable discussion. That is quite proper. If hon. gentlemen opposite tell me that they have not exhausted the discussion on this clause, I have not any fault to find. But before we agree to an adjournment at six o'clock, I think it would be reasonable that I should expect from gentlemen on the other side a promise that they shall do their share to expedite the business.

We have made substantial progress to-day. We have passed the resolution on which this Bill is founded, given the Bill a second reading, and now we are in committee on the Bill. It is my opinion that we are scampering through this business too precipitately. Has the right hon. gentleman laid all the information in his possession before the House in respect to this matter ?

We have been collecting a great deal of information with regai d to the character of the road between Quebec and Winnipeg. I stated when I introduced the measure, that there were Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
mountains of information, and I have nothing to detract from the strength of the information that I gave then. But these mountains of information are very hard of access, and it will take a good deal of time to get at them. I have tried to condense them, however, and I hope to have a condensation of them to lay on the Table of the House.
Might I ask if, in these mountains of information, there is any information of a precise nature in reference to the rates of freight from the west to the east, particuarly on grain ?
Iam not aware that the subject of rates was ever investigated by engineers or surveyors.

But perhaps the right hon. leader of the government would be nble to bear out the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for North Norfolk, by a document supplied by Mr. Hays, the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway, to the effect that if he gets this road and all these concessions, he will be able to carry the grain of Canada over his line for less than the water rate.
Nobody takes the hon. member for North Norfolk seriously.
That would be accurate information, and I think we are entitled to it.	-
I am afraid that my hon. friend is a doubtful Thomas, and that we can never convince him.

I do not understand the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition at the present to be disposed to make a promise for the members on this side of the House as to the course they shall pursue in the discussion of this matter. Speakink for myself alone, I would be very much indisposed to have any concession made on the terms, expressed or implied, that we should be hampered in the free exercise of our best judgment as the matter proceeds I understand that it may be the feeling of all members of the House, after the laborious efforts we have been making, that time would be saved if members took a pause and a rest to-night; but I want to say most expressly that I would be very sorry indeed to see this concession granted if it is not tlie clear understanding that in connection with it we waive no privilege whatever and we make no implied promise whatever.
If it is not mutually for the convenience of both sides of the House, I do not think this side of the House wants it.

I said nothing that would imply any intention on the part of the government to curtail discussion or to prevent any hon. gentleman exercising

the legitimate powers with which he is entrusted ; but there is a way of carrying on business. I understand that the desire of the hon. gentleman is to facilitate business, and that is all I care for, and all I expected.

I presume there is no reason to believe that members on this side of the House are not as much disposed to facilitate the transaction of business as members on the other side. We are all equally anxious to go home at the earliest possible moment; but it is still more important that this matter should be properly discussed. I do not want to say anything that is not perfectly courteous to the right hon. leader of the government; but I want to prevent any possible implication that in' whatever the right hon. gentleman may decide upon there is any understanding that we shall be bound in any way.

As I see the hon. Minister of Labour is in his place in the House, might I ask the Prime Minister if it is the intention that the House shall adjourn over Monday next on account of its being a statutory holiday ?

No, it is the intention of the government that the House shall sit on Labour Day. If my hon. friend had been in the House some few years ago, at the time Sir John Macdonald was Premier, he would remember that we sat once or twice on Dominion Day.

We had not a Minister of Labour then, nor a Labour Day.
Progress reported.
On motion of the Prime Minister, House adjourned at 0 p.m.

Thursday, September 3, 1903.
